summary: Counsel round 7: 4 staff Swift/AR reviewers (Opus) + 1 industry researcher (Opus), under strengthened supervisor duties

soundAreas: D1 VERIFIED CLOSED — round-5 root cause ("a write parks a task forever"): traced end to end. `FirebaseDropStore.save` (FirebaseDropStore.swift:75-86) awaits a non-throwing `FirestoreAcked.setData`; `race` (FirestoreAcked.swift:76-98) always adds a `Task.sleep(10s)` child, so `group.next()` resolves within the deadline on every branch — no bare continuation remains anywhere in the file. `performCloudSync` catches `.ackTimedOut` (DropStore.swift:614) and falls through to the `defer` at :603-605 which nils `syncTasks[drop.id]`, so `reconcileCloud`'s `where syncTasks[id] == nil` filter (:563) admits the retry. Registry does clear.

D1 VERIFIED — registry ownership is airtight against a stale slot. `performCloudSync`'s entry guard (DropStore.swift:602) returns BEFORE the `defer` is registered, which would leave `syncTasks[id]` populated forever — but every path that can make that guard fail (`enqueueCloudSync` :590-592, `remove` :523-525) bumps `syncGenerations[id]` first and either installs a newer task in the slot or nils it explicitly (:525). The slot is therefore always owned by the newest generation, which does register the defer. I could not construct a stuck-registry interleaving.

D1 VERIFIED — the `stagingError` capture IS synchronous and race-free. `AsyncThrowingStream.init(_:bufferingPolicy:_:)` takes a NON-escaping build closure and invokes it inline during init, so the `catch` at FirestoreAcked.swift:48-51 has fully written `stagingError` before line 53 reads it; the escaping Firestore completion closure never touches that variable. Encode-throw → `.rejected` (never `.queuedLocally`) holds as claimed.

D1 VERIFIED — no lost-ack from stream ordering. The stream's default `.unbounded` buffering means a Firestore completion that fires before the ack child begins iterating is buffered (and `finish(throwing:)` retains the terminal error), so a fast ack cannot be dropped. A completion arriving AFTER `group.cancelAll()` yields/finishes into an already-finished continuation, which is a documented no-op — safe from a crash standpoint, but it is precisely why the server's real post-deadline verdict is discarded (see findings 2 and 4).

D1 VERIFIED SAFE — double delivery / idempotent merge. `reconcileCloud` → `enqueueCloudSync` → `FirebaseDropStore.save` always writes `drops/{drop.id.uuidString}` with `merge: true` (FirebaseDropStore.swift:75-78), so re-pushing a drop whose earlier timed-out write later commits converges on the same document — no duplicate rows, no field loss. Reactions cannot auto-double-deliver: `ReactionService.send` is called only from the tap handler (ReactionSession.swift:185-197) and there is no retry loop. NOTE for the future: `DropReaction.id` is a fresh UUID per call (ReactionService.swift:11), so any auto-retry added later WOULD create duplicate reaction documents; that seam is unprotected today.

D1 VERIFIED CLOSED — ritual/receipt split. `didReact` (ReactionSession.swift:55-63) calls `startWrap(seconds: 15)` on the tap with zero network dependency; all three outcome setters gate on `token == sendToken` (:66-81); `startWatching` bumps `sendToken` (:33) so an in-flight send for a previous drop is stale. `ReactionSessionTests.testStaleTokenCannotRepaintDelivery` genuinely executes the guard (it asserts `.sending` survives an older token's `reactionFailed`) — non-vacuous per D3.

D1 VERIFIED CLOSED — terminal-verdict discipline. `enqueueCloudSync` no longer calls `clearTerminal` (DropStore.swift:584-589); the only clears are the server-ack path (:610) and the referential-integrity reap (:425-429). `testEditingTerminalDropKeepsVerdictUntilAck` (DropStoreTests.swift:512-534) executes both halves — edit-while-terminal keeps the verdict, and only after `setFailSave(nil)` + `retrySync` does the ack clear it. Non-vacuous.

D1 VERIFIED CLOSED — the reap gate. `refresh` keys the destructive reap on `if case .clean = localOutcome` (DropStore.swift:419) and `LocalDropStore.loadDrops` stamps `.absentFile` on the missing-file path (:128), so the round-2 outbox wipe through the absent-file side door cannot recur. `testOrphanedPendingIDReapedOnlyAfterProvablyCleanLoad` (DropStoreTests.swift:399-431) drives two REAL `LocalDropStore` instances over distinct temp URLs and asserts both directions — non-vacuous. The round-4 vacuity is genuinely fixed: `FlakyLocalStore` now adopts `LocalStoreDiagnostics` (DropStoreTests.swift:650-662), so the `if let localDiagnostics` branch (DropStore.swift:362) is reachable from tests.

D1 VERIFIED CLOSED — `seedProfile` single-flight and non-destructive. `seedTask == nil` is part of the snapshot guard (AccountService.swift:61), the task nils itself on completion (:68), and `guard profile == nil` brackets every attempt on both sides of the await (:89, :93). `.queuedLocally` returns without writing `profile` (:98-101), as claimed. I chased the obvious concern — that the timeout collapses the round-2 bounded retry to a single attempt — and it self-heals: the pending local mutation makes the cached user doc `exists`, so the listener sets `profile` from it, and a later server-side rejection reverts the mutation and produces a fresh `!exists && !isFromCache` event that re-arms the seed. Not a finding.

D1 VERIFIED CLOSED — persistError slot discipline. `showPersistError(_:critical:)` (GeoARSessionManager.swift:89-95) refuses to let a non-critical message overwrite a visible critical one, and both asset-failure call sites gate on `announcedFailedAssets.insert(name).inserted` (GeoARSessionManager.swift:334, 1526) so each failed asset announces once per session rather than once per re-placement. No test covers this (it needs a live AR session); flagging as a Wave A manual-verification item, not a finding.

D3 NOTE on the new suite — `testAckTimeoutKeepsPendingSilentlyAndAllowsRetry` (DropStoreTests.swift:436) is non-vacuous but it does NOT test the seam: `GatedCloudStore.save` throws `DropStoreError.ackTimedOut` directly, so `FirestoreAcked.race` is never entered. Likewise `testTombstoneRetiredWhenCloudConfirmsAbsence` (:457) never models cache-vs-server provenance — the double's `loadDrops` always "succeeds". FirestoreAcked v2 currently has ZERO direct test coverage; `race` is `private`, so there is no seam to test it through (see additional test 1).

D5 RESIDUAL CHECK — nothing in round 6 makes the recorded end-state targets (SQLite outbox, listener-diff, Cloud-Function seeding, SIWA linking) harder. The one exception is finding 3: the Wave A rules deployment is no longer a pure infra step, because deploying the committed v3 file breaks a shipping reaction button.

MINOR (no finding filed): `WriteOutcome` is declared `Sendable` with an `Error` payload (FirestoreAcked.swift:12-16); `any Error` is not Sendable, so this compiles only because the target is in Swift 5 language mode. It will fail the Swift 6 migration — worth a residual note, not a defect today.

findings.claim: Cancellation of a FirestoreAcked write resolves to `.acked`, not `.queuedLocally` — the seam fabricates a server confirmation for a write the server never saw, and the `catch is CancellationError` handler that implements the documented contract is largely unreachable.
findings.evidence: `AsyncThrowingStream.Iterator.next()` installs a task-cancellation handler that TERMINATES the stream by resuming the pending continuation with `nil`; it does not throw `CancellationError`. So when the ack child task is cancelled — by `group.cancelAll()` at FirestoreAcked.swift:90, or by the enclosing caller task being cancelled — `for try await _ in ack` (line 82) exits normally and falls through to `return .acked` at line 83, whose comment asserts "stream finished cleanly = server confirmed". `group.next()` (line 89) returns the FIRST child to complete; the ack child is added first (line 81) and is resumed first by cancellation propagation, so it beats the sleep child's `CancellationError`. That makes the `catch is CancellationError { return .queuedLocally }` at line 93 — the only implementation of the "Caller cancellation resolves to queuedLocally" contract documented at lines 74-75 — dead in the common case. The blast radius is masked today only by accident: the only cancellers are `DropLibrary.enqueueCloudSync` (DropStore.swift:592) and `remove(_:)` (DropStore.swift:524), and both bump `syncGenerations` first, so `performCloudSync`'s post-await guard (DropStore.swift:608) discards the fabricated success. The other three callers — `AccountService.seedProfile` (AccountService.swift:90), `AccountService.updateProfile` (:131) and `ReactionService.send` (ReactionService.swift:53) — consume the outcome directly with no generation guard; they simply never cancel today.
findings.failureScenario: A user edits a drop's scale slider twice within a second while riding an elevator (no signal). The first `enqueueCloudSync` task is cancelled at DropStore.swift:592; `FirestoreAcked.setData` returns `.acked`; `FirebaseDropStore.save` returns success (FirebaseDropStore.swift:81) for a write that is still sitting unflushed in Firestore's local queue. Today only the generation guard at DropStore.swift:608 stops the library from calling `clearPending`+`clearTerminal` and rendering "Synced — the server has confirmed your drops". The moment anyone adds task-scoped cancellation to the profile or reaction path — e.g. cancelling `seedTask` on sign-out, the obvious next change given the SIWA-linking residual — `seedProfile` will set `profile = starter` (AccountService.swift:96) on a fabricated ack and latch a profile the server rejected, and `ReactionService.send` will return `.delivered`, painting "Sent to <sender>" for a reaction nobody received. That is the exact class of lie round 4's flows-6 seam was created to abolish.
findings.proposedFix: Distinguish stream-exhaustion from cancellation in the ack child. In `race`, change the child body to: `for try await _ in ack { return .acked }; return Task.isCancelled ? .queuedLocally : .acked`, and add the same check at the top of the child before iterating. Additionally, do not rely on the loser's error to signal cancellation — wrap the whole `race` in `withTaskCancellationHandler` or check `Task.isCancelled` immediately before `return first` (line 91) and downgrade `.acked` to `.queuedLocally` when the enclosing task is cancelled. Separately, either delete or correct the comment on line 83, which currently asserts the false invariant.

testCase.name: testCancelledWriteReportsQueuedLocallyNotAcked
testCase.steps: Make `race` internal (drop `private` on FirestoreAcked.swift:76) so `@testable import` can reach it. Build an `AsyncThrowingStream<Void, Error>` capturing its continuation in an outer `var` and never finishing it (models a write staged offline). Start `let t = Task { await FirestoreAcked.race(stream, timeout: 600) }`, `await Task.yield()` twice, then `t.cancel()`. Assert `await t.value == .queuedLocally` and that the value arrives in well under the 600 s timeout (proving the task did not park). Currently this returns `.acked`.
testCase.infrastructure: Needs one visibility change: `private static func race` → `static func race` (or a `#if DEBUG` test hook). No doubles required — `AsyncThrowingStream` is the whole fixture.

findings.claim: Tombstone retirement treats ANY completed cloud read as server proof of absence, but Firestore serves `getDocuments()` from the local cache when offline — and that cache already has our own unflushed delete applied. Every offline delete therefore retires its own tombstone and destroys its own retry budget on the very next refresh.
findings.evidence: `refresh` sets `cloudReadSucceeded = true` (DropStore.swift:376) purely on `cloud.loadDrops` returning, and `FirebaseDropStore.loadDrops` (FirebaseDropStore.swift:32-37) issues `getDocuments()` with the default source and never inspects `snapshot.metadata.isFromCache` — the exact check `AccountService` uses at AccountService.swift:59 to separate "server-confirmed absence" from "don't know yet". Offline, `getDocuments()` succeeds from cache and the cache has our pending delete mutation applied, so the deleted id is GUARANTEED absent from `cloudIDs` (:377). The retirement loop at :403-407 then calls `clearPendingDelete(id)` (erasing the durable UserDefaults tombstone via :692-695) and `deleteAttempts[id] = nil`, and it runs BEFORE `reconcileCloud()` at :431, so the replay at :568-571 never fires. The condition the round-6 comment calls "the disappearance of the condition that produced the verdict" is satisfied vacuously by our own act. `launchCloudDelete` also constructs a `ghost` GeoDrop with `ownerUid == nil` (:634), so `FirebaseDropStore.delete`'s owner backstop (FirebaseDropStore.swift:95) cannot compensate.
findings.failureScenario: A user deletes a link-shared drop on the subway. `FirestoreAcked.delete` hits the 10 s deadline → `.queuedLocally` → `ackTimedOut` → the tombstone is correctly kept (DropStore.swift:642-644). The user switches to the Map tab; `MapScreen.swift:105` fires `library.refresh`, the cache read succeeds, the row is absent, and "Delete confirmed by absence — retired tombstone" is logged while the server has never heard of the delete. If the staged delete is later refused — under the CURRENTLY DEPLOYED v2 rules a delete aimed at an absent doc is permission-denied, and a delete whose ownerUid no longer matches (backup restore issues a new anonymous UID, keychain is ThisDeviceOnly) is denied too — nobody observes the refusal: the task ended at the deadline and the Firestore completion fires into a stream already finished by `group.cancelAll()`. `deleteAttempts` never increments, the unresolved-set ladder never engages, and there is no code path left that will ever retry. The user believes the drop is deleted; the magic link they sent stays live indefinitely.
findings.proposedFix: Require server provenance for retirement. Extend the cloud read to report it — either widen `DropStore.loadDrops` to return provenance, or add `protocol CloudReadProvenance: AnyObject { func lastReadWasFromCache() async -> Bool }` adopted by `FirebaseDropStore` (returning `snapshot.metadata.isFromCache`) and consulted in `refresh` alongside `cloudReadSucceeded`. Gate DropStore.swift:402 on `cloudReadSucceeded && !cloudReadWasFromCache`. Belt-and-braces: also require `deleteTasks[id] == nil` so a retirement can never race an in-flight delete for the same id.

testCase.name: testOfflineCacheReadDoesNotRetireATombstone
testCase.steps: Add a drop; `await cloud.setFailDelete(DropStoreError.ackTimedOut, for: drop.id)`; `try await library.remove(drop)`; assert `pendingDeleteIDs` contains the id. Then `await cloud.setLoadResult([])` and `await cloud.setLoadFromCache(true)`; `await library.refresh(near: nil)`; assert `library.pendingDeleteIDs.contains(drop.id)` is STILL true and that a subsequent `reconcileCloud()` produces another delete attempt. Then `await cloud.setLoadFromCache(false)`; `await library.refresh(near: nil)`; assert the tombstone is now retired. The first assertion fails today.
testCase.infrastructure: Needs the provenance seam from the fix: add `CloudReadProvenance` and have `GatedCloudStore` adopt it with a settable `setLoadFromCache(_:)`. No other doubles needed — `GatedCloudStore` and `makeLibrary` already exist (DropStoreTests.swift:584).

findings.claim: The committed v3 rules' reaction emoji allow-list does not match the emoji the shipping reaction bar offers: 😂 is offered by the UI and forbidden by the rules, while 🎉 and 😭 are permitted but unreachable. Deploying the committed rules kills one of the four buttons on the loop's payoff surface.
findings.evidence: `ReactionSession.swift:21` ships `static let reactions = ["❤️", "😂", "🥹", "🤯"]`, and `ReactionOverlay` renders a button per element (ReactionSession.swift:180). `web/firestore.rules:58` permits `request.resource.data.emoji in ['❤️', '🎉', '😭', '🤯', '🥹']`. The intersection is three of four. There is no shared constant, no generation step, and no test binding the two. Worse for D3: the NEW `ReactionSessionTests` exercise `session.didReact("🎉")` at ReactionSessionTests.swift:29 and :55 — an emoji the app can never send — so the round-6 suite is written against the rules' list and structurally cannot detect the drift.
findings.failureScenario: The moment Wave A deploys the committed rules, every 😂 tap is permission-denied. `FirestoreAcked.setData` returns `.rejected` → `ReactionService.send` throws (ReactionService.swift:66) → `session.reactionFailed(token:)` → the pill reads "Couldn't send — tap an emoji to retry" (ReactionSession.swift:232). Retrying the same emoji fails identically, so the user's only escape is to notice that a different emoji works. 25% of reaction taps fail permanently for 100% of users, the sender never gets the toast, and it lands on the one surface the product route calls the loop's payoff. Note against D5: this is not "Wave A hasn't deployed yet" — it is round 6 committing a rules file that contradicts the shipping client, which converts the Wave A deployment gate from an infra step into a breaking change.
findings.proposedFix: Make one list authoritative. Keep `ReactionSession.reactions` as the source and paste exactly those four emoji into web/firestore.rules:58 (❤️, 😂, 🥹, 🤯), or drop the `emoji in [...]` clause entirely and validate `request.resource.data.emoji.size() <= 8` instead — the allow-list is buying very little security relative to the drift risk it creates. Whichever is chosen, add the drift test below so the two can never separate again.

testCase.name: testEveryShippedReactionIsPermittedByTheCommittedRules
testCase.steps: Read the bundled rules text, regex-extract the array literal following `request.resource.data.emoji in ` , split on `'`, and assert `Set(ReactionSession.reactions).isSubset(of: extracted)`. Fails today on 😂. (Optionally also assert equality, to catch the reverse drift of 🎉/😭.)
testCase.infrastructure: Needs `web/firestore.rules` added to the AugmentMeRealityTests target's Copy Bundle Resources phase so `Bundle(for: type(of: self)).url(forResource: "firestore", withExtension: "rules")` resolves. No doubles, no network, no emulator.

findings.claim: `.queuedLocally` is a terminal verdict in every caller — nothing re-checks the ack, so a write that commits at T+11 s on a slow-but-online network leaves the offline story on screen until an unrelated refresh re-uploads the whole document. The seam's own comment promises an ack re-check that no caller implements.
findings.evidence: FirestoreAcked.swift:27-28 states "callers keep their pending state and retry the ACK check later, not the write". No such re-check exists anywhere. `performCloudSync`'s `catch DropStoreError.ackTimedOut` (DropStore.swift:614-617) simply keeps the id in `pendingSyncIDs`; the only exit is `reconcileCloud()` (:431) re-WRITING the entire document, and that runs only at the end of `refresh()` — i.e. on a Map-tab appear (MapScreen.swift:105), the Sent-tab toolbar button (DropsListScreen.swift:26), or a uid change (RootView.swift:157). `AccountService.updateProfile` sets `statusText = "Profile saved on this device — syncing when online"` (AccountService.swift:138) and nothing ever clears it: the snapshot listener at AccountService.swift:46-72 writes `profile` but never touches `statusText`, so the only clear is a subsequent profile edit. `ReactionSession` paints "Will send to <sender> when you're back online" (ReactionSession.swift:231) with no correction path at all. Round 6 traded round 5's "parks forever" for "reports offline forever"; the ack that lands one second past the deadline is discarded into a finished stream (FirestoreAcked.swift:90).
findings.failureScenario: A user drops an AR surprise at a crowded venue — the app's core scenario — where Firestore acks in 12 s. Profile shows "Uploading 1 drop…" (ProfileScreen.swift:99) instead of "Synced"; ShareDropSheet shows "Still uploading — the link starts working once your drop reaches the cloud" (ShareDropSheet.swift:147) for a link that already works, discouraging them from sending it; and if they edit their display name in the same session they are told their device is offline while it is not. Recovery requires switching to the Map tab, which re-uploads the whole document and — on the same congested network — times out again, producing a re-write loop that costs bandwidth on exactly the connection that is already saturated.
findings.proposedFix: Give `.queuedLocally` a cheap resolution path instead of a re-write. Have `FirestoreAcked` return the pending outcome as an awaitable handle (e.g. `(outcome: WriteOutcome, lateAck: Task<WriteOutcome, Never>?)`) so a caller can observe the eventual verdict at low priority without re-issuing the write; or, per-caller, observe the document's own metadata: `document.addSnapshotListener(includeMetadataChanges: true)` and treat `!snapshot.metadata.hasPendingWrites` as the ack. The minimum viable fix for the two durable surfaces is (a) clear `AccountService.statusText` from the profile listener when `!snapshot.metadata.hasPendingWrites`, and (b) make `reconcileCloud`'s re-push of an `ackTimedOut` id a metadata check rather than a full `setData`.

testCase.name: testLateAckClearsPendingWithoutASecondFullUpload
testCase.steps: Add a drop against a cloud double whose `save` reports the timeout but exposes a late ack: `await cloud.setAckLate(true)` makes `save` throw `DropStoreError.ackTimedOut` while recording the id; assert `library.pendingSyncIDs.contains(drop.id)` and `saveAttempts == 1`. Then `await cloud.deliverLateAck(for: drop.id)`; `try await waitUntil { !library.pendingSyncIDs.contains(drop.id) }` and assert `saveAttempts == 1` — the pending state cleared from the ack, not from a re-upload. Fails today (the id never clears without a second save).
testCase.infrastructure: Cannot be expressed against the current `DropStore` protocol — that is part of the finding. Needs the seam from the fix: a `LateAckReporting` protocol (`func lateAcks() -> AsyncStream<UUID>`) that `GatedCloudStore` adopts with a `deliverLateAck(for:)` driver and `DropLibrary` consumes to clear pending.

findings.claim: The new share-refusal revalidation pushes the SHARED form of the drop (visibility "link", recipientName) to the cloud without ever persisting it locally, so a successful revalidation leaves local and cloud permanently divergent — and the divergence silently disables the sender's reaction listener for that drop.
findings.evidence: The refusal branch calls `library.retrySync(sharedDrop)`, and `sharedDrop` (ShareDropSheet.swift:173-178) is a copy with `visibility = "link"` and `recipientName` applied. `retrySync` (DropStore.swift:462-464) forwards straight to `enqueueCloudSync`, which never touches `drops` or `local.save` — it only launches `performCloudSync` → `cloud.save(sharedDrop)` (DropStore.swift:607), which writes `visibility: "link"` into the cloud record (FirebaseDropStore.swift:61-68). The happy path two lines below does the opposite and correctly persists first: `try await library.update(sharedDrop)` (ShareDropSheet.swift:195). `GeoDrop.visibility` defaults to `"private"` (GeoDrop.swift:64), so the local row keeps saying "private" after a successful revalidation.
findings.failureScenario: A user's drop carries a terminal verdict that is stale — the account was relinked, so the mismatch is gone. They tap "Send the magic link"; the guard fires, they see "This drop can't upload from this account connection", and the background revalidation acks. The server doc is now `visibility: "link"`; `library.drops` and drops.json still say `"private"`. `ReactionService.watchedDrops` (ReactionService.swift:75-83) filters the LOCAL array on `visibility != "private"`, so `listenKey` (:91-96) never includes this drop and the sender's `.task(id:)` in RootView.swift:148 never subscribes to its reactions. If the user then shares the link (the verdict has since cleared), the recipient's reaction IS written and IS permitted by the v3 rules — and the sender's toast, the loop's payoff, never fires. As a secondary effect the drop is simultaneously in `terminalSyncFailureIDs` and `pendingSyncIDs`, so the row shows the xmark badge while the sheet's own caption claims it can't upload.
findings.proposedFix: Persist before revalidating, or revalidate what is actually stored. Either replace line 189 with `Task { try? await library.update(sharedDrop) }` (which persists locally and enqueues the sync through the one path that keeps both sides in step), or pass the unmodified `drop` to `retrySync` so the revalidation is a pure re-attempt of the row that already exists on disk. Prefer the former — it matches what the user just asked for.

testCase.name: testShareRefusalRevalidationDoesNotDivergeLocalAndCloud
testCase.steps: Build `makeLibrary(local: FlakyLocalStore(), cloud: GatedCloudStore())`. `await cloud.setFailSave(DropStoreError.ownedByAnotherAccount, for: drop.id)`; `try await library.add(drop)`; `waitUntil { library.terminalSyncFailureIDs.contains(drop.id) }`. Build `var shared = drop; shared.visibility = "link"`. `await cloud.setFailSave(nil, for: drop.id)`; `library.retrySync(shared)`; `waitUntil { !library.terminalSyncFailureIDs.contains(drop.id) }`. Assert `library.drops.first { $0.id == drop.id }?.visibility == "link"` and that a reload from `FlakyLocalStore` agrees. Both assertions fail today (the local row stays "private").
testCase.infrastructure: Fully executable with the existing doubles — `GatedCloudStore`, `FlakyLocalStore`, `makeLibrary`, `waitUntil` are all already in DropStoreTests.swift. No new seam required.

findings.claim: The `notFound` delete branch is unreachable under BOTH the deployed v2 rules and the committed v3 draft, and the round-6 comment that justifies keeping it states a mechanism that does not exist — it replaces the old folklore with new folklore.
findings.evidence: The comment at FirebaseDropStore.swift:107-111 claims the v3 rules make this "the real success path once Wave A deploys them". But `web/firestore.rules:51-52` allows delete when `resource == null`, and a Firestore delete of a non-existent document that the rules PERMIT is a no-op success — the server acks it, so `race` returns `.acked` and control leaves at line 101, never reaching the `notFound` case. Under the deployed v2 rules the same delete is permission-denied, an NSError with `FirestoreErrorCode.permissionDenied.rawValue`, which also does not match the `where` clause at :105-106. So the branch is dead in both worlds; the only difference v3 makes is which of the two LIVE paths (`.acked` vs `.rejected`) is taken.
findings.failureScenario: The direct harm is to the next reviewer, who will read the comment and trust a mechanism that cannot fire. The live consequence it hides: today, on v2, deleting a drop that was never uploaded (created offline, sync still pending) produces three permission-denied refusals, burns the whole `deleteAttempts` budget (DropStore.swift:652-659), and lands the id in the durable `unresolvedDeleteIDs` set — a permanent "unresolved delete" record for an intent that was always satisfied. That interacts badly with finding 2, which then retires it on the first cache-served read, so the two defects mask each other's symptoms and neither surfaces in the logs as what it is.
findings.proposedFix: Delete the `notFound` case and replace the comment with the truth: under v2 an absent-doc delete returns permission-denied and is indistinguishable from a real refusal at this seam, and under v3 it simply acks. If the v2 window matters before Wave A deploys, handle it explicitly: when the delete is rejected AND the library holds no evidence the doc was ever uploaded (the id was still in `pendingSyncIDs` when `remove` ran), treat the intent as satisfied rather than spending a refusal.

testCase.name: testAbsentDocumentDeleteIsSatisfiedNotRefused
testCase.steps: Add a drop while the cloud save is gated (never acked) so it is still in `pendingSyncIDs`; `try await library.remove(drop)` with the cloud double configured to reject the delete with an NSError carrying `FirestoreErrorDomain` / `permissionDenied`; assert the id does NOT accumulate `deleteAttempts` and never reaches `unresolvedDeleteIDs`, because the library knows the document was never uploaded.
testCase.infrastructure: The library-level half is executable with the existing `GatedCloudStore` (it already supports `setGateSaves` and `setFailDelete`). Verifying the FirebaseDropStore mapping itself needs a seam that does not exist: a `DocumentWriting` protocol wrapping `setData`/`delete`, injected into `FirebaseDropStore` in place of the direct `Firestore.firestore()` calls at :76 and :97 — otherwise this can only be checked by an emulator test in Wave A.

additionalTests.name: testRaceNeverParksAndReportsQueuedOnCancellation
additionalTests.pins: Pins the two properties the whole round turns on and that currently have zero direct coverage: (a) `FirestoreAcked.race` always returns within its deadline for a write that is never answered (the round-5 root cause), and (b) caller cancellation resolves to `.queuedLocally`, never a fabricated `.acked` (finding 1). Today the suite proves neither — every round-6 ack test throws `DropStoreError.ackTimedOut` from a DropStore double and never enters the seam.
additionalTests.steps: Three cases against a hand-built `AsyncThrowingStream<Void, Error>` whose continuation is captured in an outer var. Case 1 (never answered): continuation never finished, `race(stream, timeout: 0.2)`; assert `.queuedLocally` and measure elapsed < 1 s. Case 2 (cancellation): continuation never finished, `timeout: 600`, run in a `Task`, `await Task.yield()` twice, `cancel()`; assert `await task.value == .queuedLocally` and elapsed < 1 s — this fails today with `.acked`. Case 3 (late ack loses cleanly): finish the continuation AFTER the race has already returned `.queuedLocally` and assert no crash and no state change, documenting that the server's real verdict is discarded (the mechanism behind findings 2 and 4).

additionalTests.name: testDeleteTombstoneSurvivesUntilAServerReadConfirmsAbsence
additionalTests.pins: Pins that tombstone retirement requires SERVER provenance, closing finding 2 and preventing the round-6 retirement rule from silently re-opening the round-5 'unretirable verdict' fix in the other direction. It also pins that `reconcileCloud`'s delete replay is still reachable after an offline refresh — the property that keeps a deleted link-shared drop from staying live.
additionalTests.steps: Add a drop; `await cloud.setFailDelete(DropStoreError.ackTimedOut, for: drop.id)`; `try await library.remove(drop)`; `waitUntil { await cloud.deleteAttempts >= 1 }`; assert the tombstone exists. Offline leg: `await cloud.setLoadResult([])`, `await cloud.setLoadFromCache(true)`, `await library.refresh(near: nil)` — assert `pendingDeleteIDs` STILL contains the id, assert `library.drops` still suppresses the row, and assert a following `library.reconcileCloud()` drives `cloud.deleteAttempts` to 2 (the replay survived). Server leg: `await cloud.setLoadFromCache(false)`, `await library.refresh(near: nil)` — assert the tombstone is now retired and `deleteAttempts[id]` is cleared. The offline leg fails today.
additionalTests.infrastructure: Needs the provenance seam that finding 2's fix introduces: `protocol CloudReadProvenance: AnyObject { func lastReadWasFromCache() async -> Bool }`, adopted by `FirebaseDropStore` (returning `snapshot.metadata.isFromCache`) and by `GatedCloudStore` with a `setLoadFromCache(_:)` driver, consulted in `DropLibrary.refresh` next to `cloudReadSucceeded`. Everything else — `makeLibrary`, `waitUntil`, `GatedCloudStore` — already exists in DropStoreTests.swift.

soundAreas: D1 — TERMINAL: 'never cleared at enqueue' is CLOSED. Traced enqueueCloudSync (DropStore.swift:581-596): the round-4 `clearTerminal(drop.id)` is gone; the only surviving callers of clearTerminal are performCloudSync's post-ack success path (:610), remove() (:527) and the new clean-load reap (:427). The protecting test is NOT vacuous: testEditingTerminalDropKeepsVerdictUntilAck (DropStoreTests.swift:512-534) makes the verdict via GatedCloudStore.setFailSave(.ownedByAnotherAccount) (double at :636), then calls update() at :522 — under round-4 code the assertion at :523 would fail, so the branch is genuinely exercised.

D1 — TERMINAL: 'only a server ack clears' is CLOSED. performCloudSync :607-611 clears pending+terminal+reason only after `try await cloud.save` returns and only under the current generation guard (:608). DropStoreTests.swift:531-533 flips setFailSave(nil, for:) and waits for the verdict to drop; without the clearTerminal at :610 that wait times out, so the test executes the branch it claims.

D1 — REAP: '.clean only, absent file never reaps' is CLOSED for pending ids. localOutcome is read through the new protocol at :366 and the reap is gated `if case .clean = localOutcome` at :419. testOrphanedPendingIDReapedOnlyAfterProvablyCleanLoad (DropStoreTests.swift:399-431) drives a REAL LocalDropStore over an absent file (case 1) and a `"[]"` file (case 2); under round-4's `localReadWarning == nil` gate the absent-file case would have reaped the ghost, so the assertion at :412 is load-bearing. The protocol seam is real — LocalDropStore adopts LocalStoreDiagnostics (DropStore.swift:76) and FlakyLocalStore adopts it too (DropStoreTests.swift:650) — so round-4's vacuous `as? LocalDropStore` downcast is genuinely gone.

No test asserts a terminal id survives a non-.clean load or is reaped on a clean one; the round-6 test at :399 asserts only pendingSyncIDs. Note it also lacks the `syncTasks[id] == nil` guard its pending sibling carries at :421. I could not construct a field-reachable harm from that asymmetry (a terminal drop always has a local row, because both producers — add() and update() — write to disk before enqueueing), so I am reporting it as a coverage gap (additionalTest 1), not a finding.

D1 — TOMBSTONE RETIREMENT: the MECHANISM is CLOSED, the PREDICATE is NOT. Traced :402-412: retirement runs only inside `if cloudReadSucceeded`, clears the id from both durable sets and nils deleteAttempts. testTombstoneRetiredWhenCloudConfirmsAbsence (:457-474) and the tail of testRefusedDeleteMovesToUnresolvedAndStillSuppresses (:505-507) both drive setLoadResult([]) through the real refresh() and would fail without the new block — non-vacuous. But the predicate 'absent from cloud.loadDrops' is not 'absent from the server' — see findings 1 and 2.

D1 — UNRESOLVED MIGRATION: CLOSED. launchCloudDelete's generic catch (:645-659) increments deleteAttempts and at >=3 moves pending→unresolved and nils the counter; reconcileCloud (:568) iterates only pendingDeleteIDs, so unresolved is genuinely never retried; both sets suppress the merged map at :395-396. testRefusedDeleteMovesToUnresolvedAndStillSuppresses (:479-508) walks all three attempts through reconcileCloud and asserts suppression (:500) and retirement (:507) — it executes every branch it claims.

D1 — ackTimedOut ends the pipeline task: CLOSED. performCloudSync's empty `catch DropStoreError.ackTimedOut` (:614-617) lets the `defer` at :603-605 nil syncTasks[drop.id] while the id stays in pendingSyncIDs, which is exactly what reconcileCloud's `where syncTasks[id] == nil` (:563) needs. testAckTimeoutKeepsPendingSilentlyAndAllowsRetry (:436-453) asserts saveAttempts == 2 after reconcileCloud — that assertion is only satisfiable if the registry entry actually cleared. The delete twin (:642-644) correctly spends no attempt.
D1 — REDEMPTION: CLOSED as specified (DropStore.swift:490-494 clears both delete sets and deleteAttempts; test at :538-552 executes it), but the resulting state is harmful — finding 6.

REFRESH GENERATION DISCIPLINE — SOUND. Every await in refresh() is followed by a `guard refreshGeneration == generation` (:350, :357, :364, :367, :375, :386, :388), and there is NO await between the last guard and the whole publish/retire/reap/reconcile block (:395-431). So the new destructive blocks cannot execute against a superseded snapshot. Round 6's addition at :356-359 (hoisting the diagnostics read above the guard in the local-failure branch) genuinely closed the previously unguarded failure path.

remove() RACING AN IN-FLIGHT SYNC — SOUND. remove() bumps syncGenerations (:523) before cancelling the task (:524), and every outcome branch of performCloudSync re-checks the generation (:608, :621, :626), so a stale task that resumes after a delete cannot re-mark the drop pending or terminal, and cannot resurrect it. Verified by reading all five branches, not by inference.

FirestoreAcked.race CANCELLATION — LATENT, currently neutralised (suspected overlap with the concurrency lens, D4; not spending a slot). On caller cancellation an AsyncThrowingStream iteration returns nil rather than throwing, so the ack child falls through to `return .acked` (FirestoreAcked.swift:510) and can win group.next() ahead of the sleep child's CancellationError — i.e. a cancelled write can be reported `.acked` instead of `.queuedLocally`. It reaches no state today because every cancellation site (enqueueCloudSync :592, remove :524) bumps syncGenerations first and performCloudSync re-checks it at :608 before clearing anything. Worth hardening (`try Task.checkCancellation()` before the fallthrough) but it is not a live defect.

D3 — A ROUND-4 TEST THAT OVERCLAIMS (not a round-6 regression, flagged so it is not cited as protection). testCloudFailureIsVisibleAndStaysPending (DropStoreTests.swift:255-268) asserts syncFailureReasons[id] is populated and calls that 'visible'. Nothing renders syncFailureReasons for a non-terminal drop: ShareDropSheet.swift:139 reads it only inside the terminal branch, DropsListScreen and ProfileScreen never read it at all. The test protects a model field with no surface — directly relevant to finding 3.

D5 — RESIDUAL IMPACT. Finding 2 makes the recorded SIWA account-linking end-state HARDER, not merely unaddressed: retiring every tombstone on a uid change destroys the delete intents that linking would finally have made replayable, so by the time SIWA lands there is nothing left to replay. Findings 1 and 2 do not touch the outbox/listener-diff/Cloud-Functions residuals.

findings.claim: Tombstone retirement treats ANY cloud read that does not throw as proof of server-side absence, including a read the Firestore SDK satisfied entirely from the local cache — so a delete performed offline retires its own tombstone using its own unacknowledged write as the evidence.
findings.evidence: refresh() sets `cloudReadSucceeded = true` at DropStore.swift:376 the moment `cloud.loadDrops` returns without throwing, and :403/:408 then retire every tombstone absent from that result. FirebaseDropStore.loadDrops (FirebaseDropStore.swift:32-37) calls `getDocuments()` with the default source and never inspects `snapshot.metadata.isFromCache`, so a query the SDK serves from cache (server unreachable) is indistinguishable from a server-confirmed read. The local cache already has the pending delete applied — that is the whole point of Firestore's local write queue — so the row the tombstone is waiting on is absent from exactly the read that is used to prove it is gone. The codebase already knows this distinction is load-bearing: AccountService.swift:58-61 gates the analogous 'server-confirmed absence means first run' decision on `!snapshot.metadata.isFromCache` (Wave C, counsel PBS-7). Round 6 added a data-destroying decision on the drops path without that guard.
findings.failureScenario: User creates drop D, it syncs, they send the magic link to a friend. Later, offline (subway, plane), they delete D. remove() (DropStore.swift:511-534) deletes the local row, marks the tombstone, and launchCloudDelete stages the delete in Firestore's queue; no completion fires offline, FirestoreAcked returns .queuedLocally after 10 s, FirebaseDropStore.delete maps it to .ackTimedOut, and the tombstone correctly survives (:642-644). Still offline, the user pulls to refresh on the Sent tab (DropsListScreen.swift:26) — or simply relaunches, firing RootView.swift:157. The local read is clean; `getDocuments()` returns the cached result, which no longer contains D, and does not throw. DropStore.swift:403 retires the tombstone and erases it from UserDefaults. The only durable record of the delete intent is now gone: reconcileCloud (:568) will never replay it, and nothing suppresses D any more. On reconnect the staged mutation flushes; if the server refuses it (rules refusal, quota, or the doc having been reassigned), Firestore rolls the local mutation back, D reappears in the cache, and the next refresh merges D straight back into `drops` with no tombstone left to suppress it — the deleted drop is back in the user's library and back in AR, and the magic link they believed they had killed is live again. Every user who deletes a drop while offline hits the retirement step; the resurrection needs the flush to be refused, but the loss of the durable intent is unconditional.
findings.proposedFix: Retirement must require a SERVER-confirmed read. Widen the DropStore seam so the reconciliation read reports its provenance — e.g. `func loadDrops(near:radius:) async throws -> (drops: [GeoDrop], serverConfirmed: Bool)`, or a dedicated `func serverConfirmedIDs(...) async throws -> Set<UUID>` — and in FirebaseDropStore use `getDocuments(source: .server)` (or propagate `snapshot.metadata.isFromCache`) for it. In DropStore.swift set `cloudReadSucceeded = true` only when the read was server-confirmed. `.server` throwing while offline is the correct outcome: retirement simply must not happen offline. Leave the merge path on the existing cache-tolerant read so offline refreshes still render.

testCase.name: testTombstoneSurvivesACacheServedCloudRead
testCase.steps: Add a drop; setFailDelete(DropStoreError.ackTimedOut, for: drop.id); remove(drop); wait for pendingDeleteIDs to contain the id. Then setLoadResult([]) AND mark the double's next read as NOT server-confirmed; await library.refresh(near: nil). Assert pendingDeleteIDs still contains the id and that reconcileCloud still relaunches the delete (deleteAttempts increases). Then mark the read server-confirmed, refresh again, and assert the tombstone IS retired — so the test pins both directions, not just the negative.
testCase.infrastructure: Needs the seam the fix introduces: add `private var serverConfirmed = true` + `func setServerConfirmed(_:)` to GatedCloudStore (DropStoreTests.swift:584) and have loadDrops return it through the widened DropStore signature. Everything else — makeLibrary, waitUntil, setFailDelete's round-6 Error? signature at :599 — already exists.

findings.claim: Tombstone retirement compares against a uid-SCOPED cloud query, so absence from the read means 'not owned by the current account OR gone'. After any anonymous-UID change every tombstone and every unresolved delete is retired although the documents still exist under the old uid.
findings.evidence: cloudIDs at DropStore.swift:377 is built from FirebaseDropStore.loadDrops, whose query is `.whereField("ownerUid", isEqualTo: uid)` (FirebaseDropStore.swift:33). The retirement loops at :403 and :408 read `!cloudIDs.contains(id)` as 'the row is gone'. Under a new uid that predicate is true for EVERY drop the user ever created — the read returns an empty set for a fresh anonymous account. Both sets are then erased from UserDefaults via clearPendingDelete (:692) / clearUnresolvedDelete (:702). Nothing else in the library records who a tombstone was issued against, so the account mismatch is invisible to the retirement code. Per the platform facts, anonymous UIDs are keychain ThisDeviceOnly and do NOT survive device migration, while UserDefaults (which holds pendingDeleteDropIDs / unresolvedDeleteDropIDs) IS restored from backup — so the tombstones outlive precisely the identity that could have honoured them.
findings.failureScenario: User deletes a shared drop D; the delete is refused or unanswered, so the tombstone persists durably (the exact state rounds 4-6 built it for). The user then upgrades their iPhone and restores from backup. UserDefaults comes back, the keychain UID does not, so AccountService signs in anonymously as uid B (AccountService.swift:26-35). RootView.swift:155-162 fires refresh on the new uid; the cloud read succeeds and returns [] because B owns nothing; DropStore.swift:403 and :408 retire every tombstone and every unresolved delete in one pass and wipe them from UserDefaults. D's document is still in Firestore owned by uid A with visibility "link", and firestore.rules v3 line `allow get: if isOwner() || (signedIn() && linkVisible())` keeps it readable to anyone holding the link, permanently. The app has now forgotten the delete intent entirely — no retry, no record, no surface. Harm: content the user explicitly deleted is retained server-side and stays publicly reachable forever, for any user who deletes a shared drop and later replaces or restores their phone. This also makes the recorded SIWA account-linking residual harder: after linking there is nothing left to replay (D5).
findings.proposedFix: Stamp each tombstone with the uid it was issued under — `pendingDeleteOwnerUid: [UUID: String]`, persisted alongside the id sets — and pass the reading account into refresh (e.g. `refresh(near:as uid:)`, or inject a `uidProvider` into DropLibrary). Run the retirement loops only for tombstones whose stamped uid equals the reading uid; leave every other tombstone durable and suppressing, untouched. Combined with finding 1 the predicate becomes 'the same account got a server-confirmed read that does not contain this id', which is the only statement that actually proves the delete intent is satisfied.

testCase.name: testTombstonesFromAPreviousAccountAreNotRetiredByANewAccountsRead
testCase.steps: With the library reading uid "uid-A": add drop D, setFailDelete(refusalError, for: D.id), remove(D), drive reconcileCloud until unresolvedDeleteIDs contains D (mirrors DropStoreTests.swift:479-497). Switch the library's reading uid to "uid-B" and setLoadResult([]) (B owns nothing). await refresh(near: nil). Assert unresolvedDeleteIDs STILL contains D and that refresh did not surface D in library.drops. Then switch back to "uid-A" with setLoadResult([]) and refresh: assert it IS retired now — the same-account absence is still a valid retirement.
testCase.infrastructure: Needs the uid seam the fix introduces (a `uidProvider: () -> String?` injected into DropLibrary's init, or a uid parameter on refresh). GatedCloudStore, makeLibrary, makeDefaults and waitUntil are already sufficient for everything else; no Firebase or emulator needed.

findings.claim: The terminal state has exactly one producer — a CLIENT-side pre-check on `drop.ownerUid` — and that field is usually nil on disk, so a genuine server refusal is classified as retryable and the drop stays pending forever. In that state every round-4/round-6 terminal protection is bypassed and ShareDropSheet actively reassures the user before handing out a permanently dead magic link.
findings.evidence: DropStoreError.ownedByAnotherAccount is thrown only at FirebaseDropStore.swift:55-57, from `if let owner = drop.ownerUid, owner != uid`. ownerUid is stamped only onto the cloud-bound copy (`var stored = drop; stored.ownerUid = uid`, FirebaseDropStore.swift:58-59) — the library's copy and therefore drops.json never receive it from a save. The only ways a non-nil ownerUid reaches DropLibrary.drops are the uid-scoped cloud read (FirebaseDropStore.swift:33, where owner == uid by construction, so the check can never fire) and DropSharingService.fetchSharedDrop (DropSharingService.swift:54-55, which also sets receivedViaLink = true and is filtered out at DropStore.swift:583 before ever reaching save). So for the ordinary drop — created locally, uploaded, never round-tripped-and-re-edited — ownerUid is nil and the pre-check cannot fire. Any real server refusal (permission-denied under the committed rules v3 `allow update: if isOwner() && ...`, quota, or an App Check failure) lands instead in the generic catch at DropStore.swift:625-628, which records syncFailureReasons and leaves the drop in pendingSyncIDs indefinitely, re-pushed by reconcileCloud (:563) on every refresh. Nothing renders syncFailureReasons outside the terminal branch (ShareDropSheet.swift:139), no xmark badge appears (DropsListScreen.swift:95 keys on terminalSyncFailureIDs), and ProfileScreen.swift:92 reports it as 'Uploading 1 drop…' forever.
findings.failureScenario: User's anonymous uid changes (device migration per the platform facts) or a rules/quota refusal occurs. Their local drops carry ownerUid == nil, so accountDidChange (DropStore.swift:451-457) and reconcileCloud re-push them and the server refuses with permission-denied. performCloudSync's generic catch (:626-627) keeps each drop pending. The user opens the Sent tab: no xmark badge. They swipe to share: ShareDropSheet's caption ladder falls to line 144 and tells them 'Still uploading — the link starts working once your drop reaches the cloud'. sendLink() (ShareDropSheet.swift:186) sees terminalSyncFailureIDs empty, so the round-4 flows-3 refusal never triggers; library.update succeeds locally, showShareSheet is set, and the activity sheet hands out the link. The recipient opens it, DropSharingService.fetchSharedDrop returns nil, ReceiveScreen shows 'This drop isn't available'. The sender was explicitly reassured that the link would start working, and it never will. This is the dead-link handout that terminalSyncFailureIDs exists to prevent, reachable for every drop whose local row lacks ownerUid — which is the common case, not the edge case.
findings.proposedFix: Classify terminality from the SERVER's answer, not from a client field that is not persisted. In FirebaseDropStore.save, map NSError(FirestoreErrorDomain, .permissionDenied) — and any other non-retryable Firestore code — to a terminal error, and keep the ownerUid pre-check only as a cheap fast path. In DropStore.swift add a `catch DropStoreError.refusedByServer` branch alongside :618 that clears pending, marks terminal and records the reason. Independently, persist ownerUid: have DropLibrary write back the uid the cloud store stamped after a successful save, so the client pre-check has durable input. Until either lands, ShareDropSheet must not present a reassuring caption for a drop whose latest sync attempt recorded a syncFailureReason.

testCase.name: testANonRetryableServerRefusalIsTerminalNotPerpetuallyPending
testCase.steps: Build the library with GatedCloudStore; setFailAllSaves(with: NSError(domain: FirestoreErrorDomain, code: FirestoreErrorCode.permissionDenied.rawValue)). add(drop). waitUntil syncFailureReasons[drop.id] != nil. Assert terminalSyncFailureIDs.contains(drop.id) and pendingSyncIDs does NOT contain it — the test fails today (the drop is pending, not terminal) and passes once the refusal is classified. No new double or seam required; only FirestoreErrorDomain needs importing into the test file.

findings.claim: uploadingCount silently drops every pending write whose row is not currently loaded, and ProfileScreen's ladder falls through to 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops' when it reaches zero — so the round-4 'Uploading N…' truth is replaced by a false all-clear in exactly the failure case.
findings.evidence: uploadingCount (DropStore.swift:335-337) filters pendingSyncIDs down to ids present in `drops`. DropLibrary.init restores pendingSyncIDs from UserDefaults (:322-323) but does not load `drops` — the array is empty until a refresh completes. And refresh's local-read failure branch (:352-360) returns before `drops` is ever assigned. ProfileScreen.swift:92 tests `library.uploadingCount > 0` and the else at :104-108 renders 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops'; the ladder never consults pendingSyncIDs, localReadWarning, or unresolvedDeleteIDs. Round 4's branch (removed in this diff) tested `!library.pendingSyncIDs.isEmpty`, so this exact state used to render 'Uploading N drops…'. This is a round-6 regression, not a pre-existing gap.
findings.failureScenario: User creates three drops while offline; they persist locally and sit in pendingSyncIDs. The app is later launched into the background by a location or push event while the device is still locked, so drops.json is unreadable under NSFileProtectionComplete and Data(contentsOf:) throws. refresh() takes the catch at :352, sets localReadWarning, and returns at :360 with `drops` still empty. AccountService restored the anonymous user synchronously (AccountService.swift:22-24) so uid is non-nil; terminalSyncFailureIDs is empty; lastSyncError is nil because the cloud read never ran. The user opens the You tab and reads 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops' while three drops have never left the device. The same false all-clear renders on every cold launch during the window before the first refresh completes. Harm: the user stops retrying, believes their drops are backed up, and loses them on the next reinstall or device change — the precise false-confirmation class this wave exists to eliminate.
findings.proposedFix: Keep uploadingCount as the display count but stop letting it decide the ladder. Add to DropLibrary a single computed verdict — `var isFullySynced: Bool { pendingSyncIDs.isEmpty && terminalSyncFailureIDs.isEmpty && unresolvedDeleteIDs.isEmpty && localReadWarning == nil }` — and gate ProfileScreen's 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops' branch on it. When pendingSyncIDs is non-empty but uploadingCount is 0, render the honest string ('N drops not yet uploaded — reopen the app to retry') rather than either 'Uploading' or 'Synced'. That also closes the parallel hole where an unresolved (permanently refused) delete lets the Profile claim the server confirmed everything.

testCase.name: testProfileNeverClaimsSyncedWhilePendingWritesExist

findings.claim: The new share-sheet revalidation re-enqueues `sharedDrop` — a mutated copy carrying visibility "link" and the typed recipient name — which was never persisted locally, so a share the user was told had FAILED can still publish the drop as link-readable and leave the local store disagreeing with the cloud.
findings.evidence: sendLink()'s refusal branch (ShareDropSheet.swift:186-191) sets shareError, returns without presenting the activity sheet, and calls `library.retrySync(sharedDrop)`. `sharedDrop` is the computed copy at :173-178 with `updated.visibility = "link"` and `updated.recipientName = recipientName`. DropLibrary.retrySync (DropStore.swift:462-464) goes straight to enqueueCloudSync — it does not call local.save and does not touch DropLibrary.drops, unlike the success path at :195 which routes through update() and therefore persists. So the only place that mutation exists is the Firestore write. Under firestore.rules the published visibility is load-bearing: `allow get: if isOwner() || (signedIn() && linkVisible())` makes a "link" document readable by any signed-in user holding the id.
findings.failureScenario: A terminal verdict from a previous account connection is stale (the launch revalidation at RootView.swift:161 ran while the device was offline, so the verdict stands). The user comes back online, opens the share sheet, types a recipient name, taps 'Send the magic link', and reads 'This drop can't upload from this account connection'. No activity sheet appears; they conclude nothing was sent. Behind that message retrySync uploads the drop with visibility "link" and the recipient's name attached; the write is accepted, clearTerminal fires (:610), and the document is now link-readable by any signed-in user. The user's own device still records visibility "private" in drops.json, so nothing in the app reflects that the drop is now public-by-link, and the next local edit will silently flip it back — leaving the cloud and local copies permanently able to disagree about who can read this drop.
findings.proposedFix: Revalidate the drop AS STORED, not the un-persisted share mutation: change ShareDropSheet.swift:189 to `library.retrySync(drop)`. The revalidation's job is to test whether the account can write this document at all; it has no business publishing a visibility change the user never completed. If the share mutation should be applied, it must go through library.update (which persists locally first), on the success path only.

findings.claim: The redemption path re-admits the drop with receivedViaLink == true, which permanently marks the user's OWN drop as a viewer copy on disk — after which remove() takes the viewer early-return and deletes it locally only, creating no tombstone and no cloud delete, nondeterministically depending on whether a cloud read has run since launch.
findings.evidence: update()'s redemption block (DropStore.swift:490-494) fires on `drop.receivedViaLink == true`; the only producer of that flag is DropSharingService.fetchSharedDrop (DropSharingService.swift:55), and RootView.swift:63 persists that copy via `library.update(drop, persist: true)` — so receivedViaLink = true is written into drops.json. remove() then hits `guard cloud != nil, drop.receivedViaLink != true else { return }` at DropStore.swift:531 and returns BEFORE markPendingDelete/launchCloudDelete, and enqueueCloudSync bails at :583 for the same reason. The flag is not stable either: FirebaseDropStore.save strips it on the cloud copy (:60), so when a later refresh merges the cloud document over the local one at DropStore.swift:382 the in-memory copy has receivedViaLink == nil again while drops.json still says true. HomeScreen.swift:54 and :60 partition the UI on the same flag, so the drop also moves between the 'received' and 'in motion' sections across refreshes.
findings.failureScenario: User creates and shares drop D, deletes it, and the cloud delete is refused so a tombstone stands. Later they tap their own link from their sent-messages thread. ReceiveScreen fetches D with receivedViaLink = true, RootView.swift:63 calls update(), the tombstone is redeemed per design, and D is written back to disk flagged as a received copy. The user decides again that they want D gone and swipes to delete it. If they do so before the session's first cloud read has overwritten the in-memory copy — a cold launch, or any offline session — remove() takes the :531 early-return: the local row goes, no tombstone is created, no cloud delete is issued, and nothing is recorded anywhere. D's document stays in Firestore owned by them, visibility "link", and the magic link keeps working forever. If instead a cloud read has already refreshed the in-memory copy, the same gesture DOES delete the cloud document. Same user, same gesture, opposite outcomes depending on invisible timing. Harm: content the user deleted twice remains publicly link-readable, with no tombstone, no banner and no retry — the exact 'unretirable durable state' failure round 6 set out to eliminate, reintroduced through the redemption door.
findings.proposedFix: Do not conflate 'this drop arrived via a link' with 'I am not its owner'. Keep receivedViaLink as a transient presentation flag and gate the viewer early-returns at :531 and :583 on ownership instead — `drop.ownerUid != nil && drop.ownerUid != currentUid` — so a redeemed drop the user actually owns still gets a tombstone and a cloud delete. At minimum, in the redemption block at :490-494 clear receivedViaLink before persisting when the fetched ownerUid equals the current uid, so the user's own drop is never written to disk as a viewer copy.

soundAreas: D1 — WRAP-ON-TAP: CLOSED as a mechanism. ReactionSession.swift:55-63 `didReact` sets `sentEmoji`/`delivery = .sending`, bumps `sendToken`, and calls `startWrap(seconds: 15)` whenever `phase == .watching`; no network value is consulted. ARScreen.swift:31-34 snapshots on `phase == .memory`; RootView.swift:75-92 presents MemoryScreen off `phase == .memory`. ReactionSessionTests.swift:12-22 genuinely executes the branch (phase is `.wrapping` synchronously after the call, no await needed) — non-vacuous. The round-5 critical-1 defect (the loop's payoff gated on a server ack) is gone. It opened a new one: every reaction now reaches the Memory screen, including rejected ones, and the Memory screen is never told which — see finding 1.

D1 — QUEUED COPY: CLOSED. ReactionService.swift:59-67 maps `queuedLocally` → `.queued`; ReactionSession.swift:231 renders "Will send to <sender> when you're back online". The copy under-claims (it never asserts receipt), which is the correct direction for a truth surface.

D1 (FOCUS ANSWER) — DOES THE QUEUED PILL EVER SETTLE? No, and I judge that ACCEPTABLE. FirestoreAcked.race (FirestoreAcked.swift:507-519) calls `group.cancelAll()` after the timeout wins, so the real Firestore completion is never observed; nothing calls `reactionDelivered` afterwards and `.queued` is terminal for the session. But the pill's lifetime is bounded and short: the ack deadline is 10 s (FirestoreAcked.swift:448) while the wrap is 15 s (ReactionSession.swift:60), so the pill can show "queued" for ~5 s before `phase` flips to `.memory` and RootView.swift:75 covers it. It under-claims for those seconds and then disappears. Two nits, neither worth a slot: (a) a slow-but-online connection that acks at 11 s tells an online user "when you're back online"; (b) if the user holds to extend (ReactionSession.swift:84-87, 30 s) the stale pill lives longer. The unacceptable part is the surface that OUTLIVES the pill and does over-claim — finding 1.

D1 — PER-SEND TOKENS: CLOSED. `sendToken` is bumped in both `didReact` (ReactionSession.swift:58) and `startWatching` (:33); all three completion entry points guard on it (:67, :73, :79); ReactionOverlay.swift:183-196 captures the token at the tap and presents it on every outcome. ReactionSessionTests.swift:41-59 drives the guards for real — it asserts `delivery` stays `.sending` after a stale `.failed` and that a cross-drop ack leaves `delivery` nil. Non-vacuous. `startWatching` invalidating in-flight sends is repaint-only (it does not cancel the Task or the staged write) — correct: the reaction to the previous drop was genuinely sent and should land.

D1 — INCIDENT DISMISSAL: PARTIAL. The control exists (DropsListScreen.swift:66) and LocalDropStore.acknowledgeIncident (DropStore.swift:187-190) clears both the durable journal file and `pendingReadWarning`, so the quarantine case stays dismissed across the next load (the quarantine moved the file, so the next load is `.absentFile` → warning nil). For `.skippedRows` the banner legitimately returns on the next load because the condition genuinely persists — correct, not a defect. What is not closed is the DropLibrary wrapper: its generation guard (DropStore.swift:441) makes the visible clear a coin-flip against any concurrent refresh — finding 6.

D1 — NO RAW FILENAMES IN USER COPY: CLOSED. DropStore.swift:176 now reads "a backup was kept on this device"; the quarantine filename survives only in the log at :171, and the sidecar filename only in the log at :201. I checked every remaining user-facing string produced by the store and the library (DropStore.swift:30-35, 138, 148-149, 176, 359, 473, 504, 518, 548) — none carries a path or filename.

D1 — PER-ROW xmark BADGE: CLOSED. DropsListScreen.swift:92-96 passes `cantSync: library.terminalSyncFailureIDs.contains(drop.id)`; DropRow renders it at :154-159 with an accessibilityLabel matching the aggregate banner's wording at :39-47. One residual I am folding into finding 3's family rather than reporting separately: the aggregate count can exceed the number of visible badges, because the banner counts terminal ids while the badges can only mark ids present in `drops` (before a `.clean` load reaps the orphans).

D1 — PADDING FIX: CLOSED. DropsListScreen.swift:73-78 — the vertical-padding predicate now includes `!library.terminalSyncFailureIDs.isEmpty`. I checked it against all four `if` branches at :39-69 (terminal / lastSyncError / lastPersistError / localReadWarning); the predicate and the branch set now match exactly, so no banner can render in a zero-height inset.

D1 — LADDER CHANGE (deletions removed): VERIFIED as a code change (ProfileScreen.swift:92-111; the `pendingDeleteIDs` branch is gone) and I accept the product judgment for `pendingDeleteIDs` — a delete in flight is background cleanup and should not block a positive status. It is NOT acceptable for `unresolvedDeleteIDs`, a set round 6 created in the same change: see finding 4. `uploadingCount` (DropStore.swift:335-337) does what it claims — it filters to ids with a loadable row — but the ids it excludes land on no surface at all, so the ladder falls through to its most reassuring branch: see finding 3.

D1/FOCUS — SHAREDROPSHEET retrySync CANNOT SPIN, and the caption precedence is right. ShareDropSheet.swift:186-191 returns immediately after one `retrySync`; `enqueueCloudSync` (DropStore.swift:581-596) cancels any prior task and starts exactly one; `performCloudSync` re-marks terminal on the same error (DropStore.swift:618-624) and never re-enqueues. One tap = one attempt; no self-sustaining loop. With terminal AND pending both true the caption chain at ShareDropSheet.swift:130-155 shows `shareError` first — the honest "can't upload" text wins over "Still uploading" — correct precedence. The defect is WHAT it uploads (finding 5). Secondary nit not worth a slot: `shareError` is `@State` and is never cleared when the background revalidation succeeds, so the sheet keeps showing the refusal after the verdict has cleared; the user recovers by tapping the CTA again.

FOCUS JUDGMENT — MULTIPLE EMOJI TAPS: each-tap-a-reaction is DEFENSIBLE product semantics and I am not reporting it as a defect. `didReact` does not cancel the previous send, and `ReactionService.send` mints a fresh document id per call (ReactionService.swift:11, :50-58), so N taps = N documents, N sender toasts, N rows in the recap. For a live 15-second session that is a reaction stream, and the sender's toast per reaction IS the payoff. What is inconsistent is the presentation: the bar draws an exclusive selection ring that MOVES on each tap (ReactionSession.swift:203-212) and the pill is singular ("Sent to X"), both of which present a replace-my-one-reaction model over an append-only backend — so the viewer under-counts what the sender actually received. Copy/affordance mismatch, below the bar given the six above; worth one line in the round-7 UI pass. Flagging for whoever fixes it: the obvious dedup (a uid-keyed reaction document id) would be REJECTED by the committed rules, which set `allow update: if false` on reactions (web/firestore.rules:64) — the two changes must land together.

D1 — TERMINAL VERDICT NOT CLEARED AT ENQUEUE: CLOSED. DropStore.swift:585-589 — the enqueue-time `clearTerminal` is gone; `clearTerminal` now survives only in `performCloudSync` on a real ack (:610) and in `remove` (:527). DropStoreTests.swift `testEditingTerminalDropKeepsVerdictUntilAck` drives it end to end and is non-vacuous — it was made executable by widening `setFailSave` to `Error?` so the ack path is reachable.

D1 — REAP KEYS ON .clean ONLY: CLOSED. DropStore.swift:419 `if case .clean = localOutcome`. `testOrphanedPendingIDReapedOnlyAfterProvablyCleanLoad` drives both arms against real `LocalDropStore` files (absent path vs a file containing `[]`), and the two libraries share one injected defaults suite so case 2 genuinely re-reads the ghost that case 1 preserved (asserted before the refresh). This is a real fix for the round-4 vacuity: the `LocalStoreDiagnostics` protocol (DropStore.swift:62-67) replaced the concrete `as? LocalDropStore` downcast, and `FlakyLocalStore` now adopts it and sets `.readFailed`/`.clean` on the paths it fakes.

SCOPE NOTE (D3/D5, outside my lens but load-bearing for it): FirestoreAcked's own logic is untested. Every round-6 test reaches the ack states by having `GatedCloudStore` throw `DropStoreError.ackTimedOut` directly; nothing exercises `FirestoreAcked.race`, the 10 s deadline, the encode-throw→`.rejected` mapping, or the cancellation→`queuedLocally` mapping, because there is no Firestore document double. I traced the code and found no path that parks forever (the task group's first result wins, `cancelAll` follows, `CancellationError` maps to `queuedLocally`), but that is a reading, not a test — I expect the concurrency lens to own it.

findings.claim: The Memory screen — the loop's payoff and the only artifact the user can save to Photos — claims the reaction was received even when the send was REJECTED. Round 6's wrap-on-tap fix routes every reaction to this screen, but the screen is never told the delivery outcome, so `.delivered`, `.queued` and `.failed` render identically.
findings.evidence: RootView.swift:80-89 constructs MemoryScreen with `myReaction: reactionSession.sentEmoji` and passes no delivery state at all. MemoryScreen.swift:137-142 `reactionSummary` synthesizes a fake `DropReaction(emoji: myReaction, uid: "", byName: "")` whenever the cloud fetch at :72 returns empty — which is exactly what happens offline or after a rejection — and renders it as "❤️ ×1" in the recap at :46-52, under the headline "That made <their> day." (:40) and above "Save memory" (:58). Nothing on the screen is conditioned on `session.delivery`. This is a round-6 regression: in round 4 `reactionFailed()` did not start the wrap, so a rejected reaction never reached this screen; ReactionSession.swift:59-61 now starts it unconditionally on the tap. Timing makes it certain rather than racy — the ack deadline is 10 s (FirestoreAcked.swift:448) and the wrap is 15 s (ReactionSession.swift:60), so `delivery` is always settled to `.failed`/`.queued`/`.delivered` BEFORE this screen appears, and the screen ignores it.
findings.failureScenario: A viewer walks to a drop in a spot with no usable signal (the normal outdoor AR case) or reacts to a drop whose cloud document was never uploaded — under rules v3 the reaction create requires `get(drops/{id}).data.visibility in ['link','public']` (web/firestore.rules:60-61), so an unuploaded parent means a hard rejection. The pill flashes "Couldn't send" for a few seconds, the 15 s wrap ends, and the user lands on a confetti screen that says "SESSION CLOSED / That made Sam's day. / ❤️ ×1 from Sam" and offers to save it to Photos. Sam received nothing. The user keeps a keepsake of a delivery that never happened, and the app's most emotionally loaded surface is the one telling the lie.
findings.proposedFix: Pass `reactionSession.delivery` into MemoryScreen from RootView.swift:80-89 and branch on it. Only `.delivered` may include `myReaction` in the synthesized fallback at MemoryScreen.swift:139. For `.failed`, drop the synthesized row and add an explicit caveat line plus a retry affordance ("Your ❤️ didn't reach Sam — tap to send it now"). For `.queued`, render it as pending ("Your ❤️ sends when you're back online"), not as a count. Keep the ritual — the confetti and the watched-seconds recap are honest — and strip only the delivery claim. Bonus: gate `saveToPhotos` copy so a keepsake of an undelivered reaction does not read as a receipt.

testCase.name: testMemoryRecapNeverClaimsAReactionTheServerRefused

Then assert the table directly: summary(delivery: .delivered, allReactions: [], myReaction: "❤️") contains "❤️ ×1" and no caveat; summary(delivery: .failed, allReactions: [], myReaction: "❤️") contains NO "×" count and returns a non-nil caveat; summary(delivery: .queued, ...) returns a pending caveat and no count; summary(delivery: .failed, allReactions: [otherPersonsReaction], myReaction: "❤️") shows the other person's reaction but still no count for mine. The `.failed` case fails today.
testCase.infrastructure: None beyond the extraction seam — no Firestore, no doubles, no @MainActor harness. The logic is only untestable today because it lives inline in a private computed var on a SwiftUI View.

findings.claim: The reaction bar offers 😂, which the firestore.rules v3 draft committed in this same round does not permit. The moment Wave A deploys those rules, one of the four reaction buttons will fail every single time, and the failure copy tells the user to retry with the button that cannot work.
findings.evidence: ReactionSession.swift:21 `static let reactions = ["❤️", "😂", "🥹", "🤯"]`. web/firestore.rules:58 `request.resource.data.emoji in ['❤️', '🎉', '😭', '🤯', '🥹']`. I compared the bytes rather than the glyphs: ❤️ is `e29da4 efb88f` in both files (exact match), 🥹 `f09fa5b9` and 🤯 `f09fa4af` match, but the app's 😂 is `f09f9882` and appears nowhere in the rules list, while the rules' 🎉 `f09f8e89` and 😭 `f09f98ad` appear nowhere in the app. Nobody cross-checked the two lists — the round-6 tests themselves reach for an emoji the UI cannot produce (ReactionSessionTests.swift:29 and :55 use "🎉"). D5 puts the Wave A rules DEPLOYMENT out of scope, but this is in scope on its own terms: round 6 committed a contract that contradicts a shipped surface, which makes that deployment strictly more dangerous than it was before this round.
findings.failureScenario: The day Wave A deploys rules v3, roughly a quarter of all reaction taps — 😂 is the second button and a natural first choice — get permission-denied. `ReactionService.send` throws (ReactionService.swift:64-67), the pill reads "Couldn't send — tap an emoji to retry" (ReactionSession.swift:232), and the user does exactly that: taps 😂 again, and fails again. Meanwhile the wrap started on the tap, so 15 s later they are on the Memory screen being told it worked (see finding 1). Every viewer who prefers 😂 experiences the product's payoff as broken, and the sender never learns anyone reacted.
findings.proposedFix: Make one list the source of truth before the rules ship. Simplest: change web/firestore.rules:58 to the app's actual set `['❤️', '😂', '🥹', '🤯']`, or widen it to the union and let the client narrow. Better, and what stops the next drift: generate the rules' allow-list from `ReactionSession.reactions` at build time, or add the contract test below so the two lists cannot diverge silently again. Also fix ReactionSessionTests.swift:29/:55 to use an emoji the bar actually offers — a test that sends 🎉 is testing a tap no user can make.

In the same test, extract the `hasOnly([...])` key list at rules line 59 and compare it against the encoded keys of `DropReaction(emoji: "❤️", uid: "u", byName: "n")` via Mirror, so a future field added to DropReaction fails here instead of in production. Fails today on 😂.
