findings.claim: `unresolvedDeleteIDs` is a durable, UserDefaults-persisted state with ZERO user-facing surface anywhere in the app. Round 6 created it and, in the same round, deleted the only surface deletions ever had — so after three refusals the app stops retrying, hides the drop from the user, and reports "Synced" while the server copy stays live and readable to anyone holding the link.
findings.evidence: DropStore.swift:655-659 moves the id into `unresolvedDeleteIDs` and clears `deleteAttempts`; `reconcileCloud` at :568-571 only replays `pendingDeleteIDs`, so nothing ever retries it again. `refresh` at :396 suppresses it from `drops`, so it vanishes from the Sent list. Grepping every Swift file under AugmentMeReality/ for `unresolvedDelete` returns hits in DropStore.swift only — no view reads it. Meanwhile ProfileScreen.swift:92-111 dropped the `pendingDeleteIDs` branch entirely, so the ladder falls straight through to "Synced — the server has confirmed your drops" (:105-108). The round-5 researcher's argument ("the user considers a deleted drop deleted") justifies hiding an in-flight delete; it does not justify hiding a delete the server has permanently refused. The code comment at :646-651 states the intent is "still no resurrection" locally — but the harm is not local resurrection, it is the surviving remote copy.
findings.failureScenario: The user migrates to a new iPhone. Anonymous UIDs are keychain ThisDeviceOnly and do NOT survive device migration (stated platform fact), so the restored app has a new uid while the cloud documents still carry the old `ownerUid`. The user opens Sent, deletes a drop they regret sharing — a location, a private message to an ex — and the cloud delete is refused by the owner check three times. The row disappears locally, the tombstone goes to `unresolvedDeleteIDs`, retries stop, and Profile says "Synced — the server has confirmed your drops". The recipient's magic link keeps working forever. The user believes they deleted it; the app has no surface that could ever tell them otherwise, and no control that could retry.
findings.proposedFix: Give the set a surface and a control. Add an `unresolvedDeleteIDs` branch to the ProfileScreen ladder ABOVE `.synced` — "N drop(s) couldn't be removed from the cloud" — and a matching banner + per-row treatment on DropsListScreen (the rows are suppressed, so this needs a small 'Couldn't delete' section rather than a badge), each with a Retry that clears `deleteAttempts` and calls `launchCloudDelete`. At minimum, `unresolvedDeleteIDs.isEmpty` must become a precondition of the "Synced" branch: a durable state the app cannot resolve must never be silent. Keep the retirement paths as built (cloud-read absence at :408-411, re-receive at :490-494) — they are correct; it is the silence that is not.

testCase.name: testUnresolvedDeleteIsNeverReportedAsSynced
testCase.steps: Extract the ProfileScreen ladder into a computed `DropLibrary.syncStatus` returning an enum (.connecting / .terminalFailures(Int) / .syncError(String) / .uploading(Int) / .unresolvedDeletes(Int) / .synced) and have ProfileScreen render off it. Then reuse the exact sequence DropStoreTests already proves works in `testRefusedDeleteMovesToUnresolvedAndStillSuppresses`: GatedCloudStore + makeLibrary, add a drop, setFailDelete(refusal), remove, reconcileCloud until `library.unresolvedDeleteIDs.contains(drop.id)`. Then XCTAssertNotEqual(library.syncStatus, .synced) and assert the status carries a non-zero unresolved count. Fails today (the status is .synced).
testCase.infrastructure: Existing GatedCloudStore, makeLibrary and waitUntil helpers in DropStoreTests.swift — the refusal→unresolved drive is already proven executable there. The only new seam is the `syncStatus` extraction.

findings.claim: Swapping `pendingSyncIDs.count` for `uploadingCount` removed un-pushable pending writes from the progress count without adding them to any problem surface — so the ladder falls through to "Synced — the server has confirmed your drops" in exactly the states where the app cannot even read its own local truth and still holds an unflushed outbox.
findings.evidence: DropStore.swift:335-337 `uploadingCount` filters `pendingSyncIDs` down to ids present in `drops`. Its own comment at :332-334 says a pending id with no loadable row "is a problem, never progress" — but the code only removes it from progress; grep shows `uploadingCount` is read at ProfileScreen.swift:92/:99 and nowhere else, and no surface reads the excluded ids. The ladder at ProfileScreen.swift:92-111 therefore reaches the terminal `else` and prints "Synced — the server has confirmed your drops". Compounding it: the local-read-failure branch in `refresh` (DropStore.swift:352-360) sets only `localReadWarning` and returns before the cloud block, so `lastSyncError` stays nil — and `localReadWarning` is rendered only on DropsListScreen.swift:58, never on Profile. Round 4 showed "Uploading N drops…" here, which was over-optimistic but was not a claim of server confirmation.
findings.failureScenario: A user's drops.json becomes unreadable (disk pressure during a write, or the whole-file quarantine path at DropStore.swift:167-177) while `pendingSyncIDs` still holds two never-acked drops restored from UserDefaults at :322-323. On the next launch `refresh` aborts in the catch branch, `drops` stays empty, `uploadingCount` is 0. The user opens the You tab to check whether their drops are safe before wiping the app or switching phones — the single question this status line exists to answer — and reads "Synced — the server has confirmed your drops". The server has confirmed nothing; the app could not even open the file. Rare trigger, but it is the precise state the surface was built for.
findings.proposedFix: "Synced" must be a claim about the whole state, not the residue of one filter. Gate the terminal branch on all of: `pendingSyncIDs.isEmpty` (not `uploadingCount == 0`), `unresolvedDeleteIDs.isEmpty`, `terminalSyncFailureIDs.isEmpty`, and `localReadWarning == nil`. Give the excluded ids their own honest branch — "N drop(s) waiting to upload — couldn't be read from this device" — and render `localReadWarning` on the Profile ladder too, since Profile is where users go to ask this question and DropsListScreen is not.

testCase.name: testStatusIsNotSyncedWhenLocalTruthIsUnreadableAndTheOutboxIsNotEmpty
testCase.steps: Using the same `DropLibrary.syncStatus` extraction as the previous finding: seed a fresh defaults suite via makeDefaults() with `pendingSyncDropIDs` = [ghostUUID], build the library with `FlakyLocalStore` as the local store, `await store.setThrowOnLoad(true)`, then `await library.refresh(near: nil)`. Assert `library.localReadWarning != nil` (proves the catch branch ran), `library.uploadingCount == 0` (proves the filter excluded the ghost), and XCTAssertNotEqual(library.syncStatus, .synced). Fails today on the last assertion.
testCase.infrastructure: Existing FlakyLocalStore — round 6 already made it conform to LocalStoreDiagnostics and set `.readFailed` plus a warning on the throwing path (DropStoreTests.swift, FlakyLocalStore.loadDrops), so this branch is genuinely reachable now. Plus makeDefaults(). New seam: `syncStatus`.

findings.claim: The share-refusal path uploads `sharedDrop` — a mutated copy carrying `visibility = "link"` and the typed recipient name — even though that mutation was never persisted locally and the app has just told the user in the same breath that this drop cannot upload from this account connection. The app says one thing on screen and does the opposite in the background.
findings.evidence: ShareDropSheet.swift:186-191: the guard sets `shareError` and then calls `library.retrySync(sharedDrop)`. `sharedDrop` is the computed property at :173-178, which sets `visibility = "link"` and `recipientName`. The successful path at :195 reaches those mutations through `library.update(sharedDrop)`, which persists to disk first (DropStore.swift:500-508); the refusal path skips `update` entirely and hands the mutated value straight to `retrySync` → `enqueueCloudSync` → `cloud.save` (DropStore.swift:462-464, 581-596, 607). So if the revalidation succeeds, the server ends up with a link-visible document bearing the recipient's name for a drop the user never sent, while the local record still says `visibility = "private"` (GeoDrop.swift:64). Under the committed rules that document is then readable by any signed-in client holding its id (web/firestore.rules:40 `allow get: if isOwner() || (signedIn() && linkVisible())`), whereas a private document is owner-only. A later `refresh` merges the cloud copy back over the in-memory row once pending clears (DropStore.swift:378-383), so the app silently adopts a share the user abandoned.
findings.failureScenario: A user whose drops carry a previous anonymous uid (post-device-migration) opens the share sheet, types "Mum" as the recipient, and taps "Send the magic link". The app refuses in red — "This drop can't upload from this account connection" — and they close the sheet, believing nothing left the device. In the background the app uploads that drop with `visibility: "link"` and `recipientName: "Mum"`. The exposure is bounded by the document id being an unguessable UUID, so this is a contradiction between statement and behaviour rather than a live leak — but it is the app publishing a share the user was just told was impossible, and it flips the document from owner-only to link-readable.
findings.proposedFix: Revalidate the drop the library already holds, not a caller-mutated copy: change ShareDropSheet.swift:189 to `library.retrySync(drop)`. Better, close the seam rather than the instance — replace `retrySync(_ drop: GeoDrop)` (DropStore.swift:462-464) with `revalidateTerminal(_ id: UUID)` that looks its own row up in `drops`, so no caller can ever push an unpersisted mutation through the revalidation path. If the intent really is to carry the share forward on success, then persist it first via `update` — but then the refusal message on screen is wrong and should say the share was saved and will upload if the verdict clears.

findings.claim: The Dismiss button is unreliable in both directions because `acknowledgeReadIncident` guards on a generation it does not own: any interleaving refresh either swallows the dismissal or immediately re-posts the banner the user just dismissed — while the durable journal has already been cleared, so displayed state and stored state diverge.
findings.evidence: DropStore.swift:436-445 captures `generation = refreshGeneration` at tap, awaits the actor's `acknowledgeIncident()`, then clears `localReadWarning` only `if refreshGeneration == generation`. But `refresh` bumps that same counter on entry (:343) and every mutator bumps it too (:469, :485, :512), and `acknowledgeReadIncident` does not bump it. Two orderings, both realistic: (A) a refresh is already in flight when the user taps — the generation still matches, the warning is cleared, and then the in-flight refresh resumes at :365 and assigns `localReadWarning = warning`, a non-nil string it read from the journal at :363 BEFORE `acknowledgeIncident` deleted the file; its own generation guards at :364 all pass because the acknowledgment never bumped the counter, so the banner reappears with nothing the user can do. (B) any refresh or mutator starts after the tap — the guard at :441 fails and `localReadWarning` is never cleared, so the banner stays even though the journal is gone. Ordering B is easy to hit at launch: RootView.swift:155-162 fires a refresh on the uid task and DropsListScreen.swift:24-30 offers a refresh button on the very screen the banner lives on. This makes the round-6 answer to the round-5 concurrency-5 finding partial rather than closed.
findings.failureScenario: A user relaunches after a corruption incident, lands on the Sent tab with an empty library and the orange "Your saved drops couldn't be read — a backup was kept on this device" banner, and taps Dismiss. RootView's uid-keyed refresh is still running (it starts on appear and awaits both stores), so either the banner blinks off and back on, or it never goes away at all. The user taps Dismiss two or three more times; each tap clears the on-disk journal again but the banner stays. The one control offered for an undismissable banner is itself undismissable — and the durable incident record is now gone, so the state the banner reports and the state the store holds no longer agree.
findings.proposedFix: Treat acknowledgment as a mutator, not a bystander. Bump `refreshGeneration` at the top of `acknowledgeReadIncident` so any in-flight refresh aborts at its next guard, set `localReadWarning = nil` synchronously on the MainActor before awaiting the store (the method is already MainActor-isolated), and drop the equality guard on the async tail — the only thing that needs the await is the journal write. Then make `refresh` respect the acknowledgment: track an `acknowledgedIncidentGeneration` and skip re-posting a warning whose text was acknowledged after the load that produced it. Do not clear the journal until the visible clear has actually happened, so disk and screen cannot disagree.

Trace: no `withCheckedThrowingContinuation` survives anywhere (FirestoreAcked.swift:31-99); `race` always terminates because the sleep child (FirestoreAcked.swift:85-88) is unconditional, so the round-5 'parks forever offline' root cause is genuinely dead. Encode-throw is captured synchronously (the `AsyncThrowingStream(build:)` closure runs inline) and short-circuits before the race (:38-53) — correctly `.rejected`, not `.queuedLocally`. Routing is complete: FirebaseDropStore.swift:75 (save) and :96 (delete), ReactionService.swift:53, AccountService.swift:90 and :131. One raw write remains outside the seam the file itself declares mandatory: FirebaseHealthcheck.swift:35 `doc.setData(["healthcheck": stamp], merge: true)` — diagnostics-only, not a shipping UI path, but it contradicts FirestoreAcked.swift:20. PARTIAL: the documented contract 'Caller cancellation resolves to queuedLocally' (FirestoreAcked.swift:74-75) is NOT met. Under caller cancellation both children finish immediately; the stdlib finishes a cancelled AsyncThrowingStream iteration by returning nil, so the ack child falls through `for try await _ in ack` to `return .acked` (:82-83) and can win `group.next()` — a cancelled write can report a SERVER ACK. I traced every cancellation source before rating this: `syncTasks[id]?.cancel()` at DropStore.swift:592 and :524 are the only ones, and both bump `syncGenerations` first, so `performCloudSync`'s guards (:602, :608) discard the false ack. `deleteTasks` are never cancelled; the reaction/profile Tasks are unstructured and never cancelled. findings.claim: Round 6's new tombstone retirement treats ANY successful `cloud.loadDrops` as proof the server no longer holds the row, but that read is satisfiable from Firestore's local cache — which already reflects the pending local delete. Every offline refresh after a delete therefore destroys the durable delete record the tombstone exists to be.
findings.evidence: `cloudReadSucceeded = true` is set purely on the absence of a throw (DropStore.swift:376) and `cloudIDs` is built from the returned rows (:377); the retirement at :402-407 then does `clearPendingDelete(id)` and `deleteAttempts[id] = nil` for every id not in that set. The underlying call is `getDocuments()` with the default source (FirebaseDropStore.swift:32-34), which returns a cache-backed snapshot with `metadata.isFromCache == true` when the server is unreachable rather than throwing — and Firestore's latency compensation has already removed the locally-deleted doc from that cache. The `DropStore` protocol (DropStore.swift:10) returns `[GeoDrop]` and discards `snapshot.metadata` entirely, so `DropLibrary` structurally CANNOT tell a server answer from a cache answer: round 6 built a destructive decision on a signal the seam cannot provide. The codebase already knows this rule and applies it correctly one file away — AccountService.swift:59 gates seeding on `!snapshot.metadata.isFromCache` with the comment 'only a SERVER-confirmed absence means first run' (counsel PBS-7). Once retired, `reconcileCloud`'s replay loop (:568-571) no longer sees the id, so the client has no memory of the delete at all.
findings.failureScenario: Park visit, no signal. User deletes a drop; `launchCloudDelete` times out at 10 s and correctly keeps the tombstone (DropStore.swift:642-644). The user pulls to refresh on the Sent tab (DropsListScreen.swift:26) — still offline. The cloud read is served from cache, `cloudReadSucceeded` is true, `cloudIDs` omits the deleted id, and the tombstone plus its attempt counter are wiped. From that instant the app's only delete guarantee is Firestore's internal mutation queue, which is discarded on reinstall and is not carried across an anonymous-uid change. If that queued delete is later rejected (rules refusal, or an ownerUid that no longer matches), Firestore rolls the mutation back, the doc reappears in the cache, and the next refresh merges it into `drops` with nothing left to suppress it — the drop the user deleted is back, permanently. Frequency: every offline delete followed by any refresh, which is the app's primary field scenario.
findings.proposedFix: Make read provenance part of the seam instead of inferring it. Add `protocol CloudReadProvenance: AnyObject { func lastLoadWasServerConfirmed() async -> Bool }`, adopt it on FirebaseDropStore by recording `!snapshot.metadata.isFromCache` at FirebaseDropStore.swift:35, and require it at DropStore.swift:402: `if cloudReadSucceeded, await cloudProvenance?.lastLoadWasServerConfirmed() == true`. Cheaper interim: pass `source: .server` for the refresh query so an offline read throws instead of silently degrading — but the protocol change is what makes the invariant checkable. Do not retire on the cache under any circumstance.
