findings.claim: The same retirement predicate is evaluated against an owner-scoped query, so after any uid change every tombstone — including the new durable `unresolvedDeleteIDs` — is retired on the first refresh even though the server row is untouched. Combined with round 6 making the give-up permanent, a drop the user deleted keeps serving its magic link forever and the client never tries again.
findings.evidence: `cloudIDs` comes from `whereField("ownerUid", isEqualTo: uid).getDocuments()` (FirebaseDropStore.swift:32-34), so it can only ever contain rows owned by the CURRENT uid. Absence from it means 'not mine', not 'not there'. Round 6 nonetheless treats it as retirement proof for both sets (DropStore.swift:403 and :408). Round 6 also made the give-up durable: after 3 refusals the id moves out of `pendingDeleteIDs` into the persisted `unresolvedDeleteIDs` (:655-659, :697-700), and `reconcileCloud` only ever replays `pendingDeleteIDs` (:568) — so unlike rounds 4/5, where `deleteAttempts` was in-memory only (:298) and every relaunch bought 3 fresh attempts, the delete is now never retried again on any future launch. The cloud delete itself is fired at the server with a synthesised ghost whose `ownerUid` is nil (:634-635), so FirebaseDropStore's owner backstop (:95) does not stop it — the server refuses it instead, under BOTH v2 and v3 rules (firestore.rules:51-52 requires `resource.data.ownerUid == request.auth.uid`). D4: this shares a code site with finding 1 but is a different mechanism with a different fix, and it fires even when every read is server-confirmed.
findings.failureScenario: User upgrades to a new iPhone. The app container restores, so the local JSON library and the persisted tombstone/terminal sets survive, but the anonymous uid does not (keychain ThisDeviceOnly), so the app signs in as a new uid. The user deletes a drop they had previously shared by link. `launchCloudDelete` fires at the old-uid document; the server refuses it 3 times; the id lands in `unresolvedDeleteIDs`. On the very next refresh the cloud read — correctly server-confirmed, returning only new-uid drops — does not contain the id, so DropStore.swift:408 'resolves it by absence' and drops the record. Net result: the document is still live on the server with `visibility: "link"`, the magic link the user sent to a friend still opens the drop, the app shows no trace of an unfinished deletion (round 6 removed deletions from the Profile ladder), and no future launch will ever retry. The user believes they deleted it. Frequency: every device migration or keychain loss with a non-empty library — a routine annual event, not an exotic state.
findings.proposedFix: Retirement must be evidence about the specific document, not about a scoped query. Replace the `!cloudIDs.contains(id)` predicate at :403 and :408 with a per-document server check — add `func confirmAbsent(_ id: UUID) async throws -> Bool` to the cloud seam, implemented as `getDocument(source: .server)` and returning `!snapshot.exists` — and run it only for ids actually in a tombstone set (bounded, and only when a retirement is being considered). Independently, stop `launchCloudDelete` from synthesising an owner-less ghost (:634-635): carry the real `ownerUid` in the tombstone so a delete aimed at a foreign-owned document is recognised as un-deletable-from-here and surfaced to the user rather than burned as three anonymous refusals.

testCase.name: testAbsenceFromAnOwnerScopedReadDoesNotRetireATombstone
testCase.steps: Add a drop; refuse its delete three times through `reconcileCloud` until `unresolvedDeleteIDs.contains(drop.id)`; then `await cloud.setLoadResult([])` while `await cloud.setDocumentStillExists(drop.id, true)` and `await library.refresh(near: nil)` — assert `unresolvedDeleteIDs` STILL contains the id and that the drop is still suppressed from `library.drops`. Then `await cloud.setDocumentStillExists(drop.id, false)`, refresh, and assert it is retired. This is the deliberate inverse of the shipped `testTombstoneRetiredWhenCloudConfirmsAbsence` (DropStoreTests.swift:457), which passes today only because the double cannot express 'the row exists but my query cannot see it'.
testCase.infrastructure: GatedCloudStore gains a `documentsOnServer: Set<UUID>` plus `setDocumentStillExists(_:_:)` and an implementation of the new `confirmAbsent(_:)` seam method. Existing `setLoadResult`, `setFailDelete`, `deleteAttempts` cover the rest.

findings.claim: The committed rules v3 draft constrains reactions to a fixed emoji set that does not match the set the shipped UI offers: the client sends 😂, which v3 does not permit, and v3 permits 🎉 and 😭, which the client never sends. Deploying v3 in Wave A silently breaks one of the four reaction buttons — 25% of every reaction tap — and offline the failure is invisible because the app has already promised delivery.
findings.evidence: `static let reactions = ["❤️", "😂", "🥹", "🤯"]` (ReactionSession.swift:21) versus `request.resource.data.emoji in ['❤️', '🎉', '😭', '🤯', '🥹']` (web/firestore.rules:58). 😂 (U+1F602) is absent from the rules list. Nothing in the app derives one from the other and nothing checks them against each other — the rules file is not in the test bundle and there is no shared constant. The ReactionSessionTests written in the same round use '🎉' (ReactionSessionTests.swift:1286, :1312), an emoji the UI never offers, which is a fingerprint of the two lists being authored independently. The rest of the reactions create rule is compatible: `hasOnly(['id','emoji','uid','byName','at'])` matches `DropReaction`'s five encoded properties exactly (ReactionService.swift:10-16). Note the exact-string comparison also makes this fragile to variation selectors — ❤️ matches only if both files carry U+2764 U+FE0F identically.
findings.failureScenario: Wave A deploys the committed rules. Online, a viewer taps 😂: `FirestoreAcked.setData` returns `.rejected`, `ReactionService.send` throws (ReactionService.swift:64-66), and the pill honestly reads 'Couldn't send — tap an emoji to retry' — but it says nothing about WHICH emoji, so the user retries 😂 and fails again, and the loop's payoff is dead for a quarter of taps with no diagnosis anywhere. Offline is worse and is the round-6-specific harm: the write stages, the 10 s deadline elapses, `send` returns `.queued`, and the pill promises 'Will send to <sender> when you're back online' (ReactionSession.swift:231). On reconnect the queued mutation is rejected by the rules and discarded by Firestore. The sender never receives it, the viewer is never told, and the app's most explicit user-facing promise in the round is broken with zero signal on either side.
findings.proposedFix: Make one side the source of truth. Hoist the allowlist to a single Swift constant (`ReactionSession.reactions`) and generate the rules literal from it in the Wave A rules build, or at minimum add `web/firestore.rules` to the test target's bundle resources and assert `Set(ReactionSession.reactions).isSubset(of: emojiAllowlistParsedFromRules)` so the two can never drift again. Immediately, before any deploy: change firestore.rules:58 to exactly `['❤️', '😂', '🥹', '🤯']`, and normalise both literals to the same variation-selector form.

testCase.name: testEveryOfferedReactionEmojiIsPermittedByTheRules
testCase.steps: Load `firestore.rules` from the test bundle, regex the `emoji in [ ... ]` literal into a `Set<String>`, and assert `Set(ReactionSession.reactions).isSubset(of: allowed)` with a failure message naming the offending emoji. Add a companion assertion that each string's unicodeScalars match between the two sources so a variation-selector drift also fails. Against today's tree this fails on 😂.
testCase.infrastructure: Add `web/firestore.rules` to the AugmentMeRealityTests target's Copy Bundle Resources. No new doubles. (The Wave A `@firebase/rules-unit-testing` suite should additionally drive one create per offered emoji, but that is a Wave A gate — this Swift test is executable today and is the one that catches the drift before deploy.)

findings.claim: Round 6 legitimised the offline reaction with an explicit promise — 'Will send to <sender> when you're back online' — but the sender-side toast filter compares the reaction's ORIGINAL client timestamp against the sender's current app-session start, so a reaction that flushes after the sender has relaunched is silently swallowed. The reaction reaches Firestore and the promise is still broken.
findings.evidence: `DropReaction.at` defaults to `Date()` stamped on the viewer's device at tap time (ReactionService.swift:16, created at :50-52), and it is written unchanged into the queued document. The sender's listener discards anything with `reaction.at > self.startedAt == false` (:118), where `startedAt = Date()` is stamped once at service construction (:25) and `ReactionService` is a `@StateObject` created per app process (RootView.swift:14). The listener is also `.order(by: "at", descending: true).limit(to: 1)` (:111), so a late-flushing older reaction is not even the newest document and cannot surface at all once any newer reaction exists. The cutoff's own comment (:98-102) is about not replaying history on re-key — it was never designed for a write whose payload timestamp predates its delivery by hours. Round 6 did not create the filter, but it is what turned an ambiguous 'Sending…' into a concrete delivery promise (ReactionSession.swift:231), so the round owns the broken promise.
findings.failureScenario: Recipient walks to the park at 14:00 with no signal, opens the magic link, reacts ❤️, sees 'Will send to Sam when you're back online', gets the Memory screen, closes the app. The write flushes when they get signal at 18:00. Sam opened the app at 17:00, so Sam's `startedAt` is 17:00 and the reaction's `at` is 14:00 — the listener drops it at ReactionService.swift:118 and Sam never gets the toast. The document is in Firestore, so it appears if Sam ever opens that drop's Memory recap (:128-134), but the live payoff the entire feature exists for never fires. Frequency: every offline reaction whose sender relaunches before the recipient reconnects — the common case, since sender and recipient are different people on different schedules.
findings.proposedFix: Filter on FIRST OBSERVATION, not on the payload timestamp. The snapshot listener already knows: treat a document whose `documentChange.type == .added` on a non-initial snapshot as new regardless of `at`, or record the highest `at` already toasted per drop in durable storage and toast anything above that watermark. Concretely, hoist the decision into a pure static beside the existing `watchedDrops`/`listenKey` statics (ReactionService.swift:75, :91) — `nonisolated static func shouldToast(_ reaction: DropReaction, myUid: String, lastToastedAt: Date?, isInitialSnapshot: Bool) -> Bool` — and drop `startedAt` from the predicate; also raise the `limit(to: 1)` so a batch of flushed reactions is not collapsed to one.

testCase.name: testAReactionStampedBeforeThisAppSessionStillToastsWhenFirstSeen
testCase.steps: Pure unit test on the hoisted predicate. Case A (the bug): `shouldToast(DropReaction(emoji: "❤️", uid: viewerUid, byName: "Ada", at: sessionStart.addingTimeInterval(-3600)), myUid: senderUid, lastToastedAt: nil, isInitialSnapshot: false)` must be true — today's `at > startedAt` logic returns false. Case B (regression guard, the behaviour the cutoff was built for): the same reaction with `lastToastedAt` already at or above its `at` must be false, and any reaction on the initial snapshot must be false, so history still does not replay. Case C: `reaction.uid == myUid` must be false (self-reactions never toast).
testCase.infrastructure: None beyond hoisting the predicate out of the closure at ReactionService.swift:112-123 into a nonisolated static, next to the two statics that already exist for exactly this reason. No Firestore, no doubles.

findings.claim: Round 6 claim (4)'s revalidation clause is not closed. Both new revalidation paths — `accountDidChange()` and the share-sheet's `retrySync` — re-run a verdict that is computed entirely from unchanged local inputs, so under the shipped anonymous-only auth model they can never clear a terminal verdict. They are recovery affordances that cannot recover, re-armed on every launch and every share attempt.
findings.evidence: A terminal verdict is only ever produced by `DropStoreError.ownedByAnotherAccount` (DropStore.swift:618-624), which `FirebaseDropStore.save` throws from a purely local comparison — `if let owner = drop.ownerUid, owner != uid` (FirebaseDropStore.swift:55-57) — with no network involved. `accountDidChange()` (:451-457) and `retrySync` (:462-464) both re-enter that same comparison with the same `drop.ownerUid` (nothing rewrites it locally; `stored.ownerUid = uid` at FirebaseDropStore.swift:59 mutates only the cloud record) and the same `Auth.auth().currentUser?.uid`. The verdict can therefore only flip if the current uid becomes equal to the drop's original uid — and anonymous uids are keychain ThisDeviceOnly, so once a migration loses one it is gone forever. The share-sheet call is additionally wrong in kind: it passes `sharedDrop` (ShareDropSheet.swift:189), a value carrying `visibility = "link"` and the just-typed `recipientName` that was NEVER persisted locally (`sendLink`'s persisting path at :195 is on the other branch), so the retry would upload a cloud state the local library does not have. Each invocation also does a real `markPending` + UserDefaults write (:584, :666-667) before failing back to terminal.
findings.failureScenario: User migrates to a new iPhone with 40 restored drops. Every launch: RootView's `.task(id:)` (RootView.swift:155-162) runs `refresh` then `accountDidChange()`, which re-enqueues all 40, does 40 markPending + 40 UserDefaults writes + 40 Tasks, and re-confirms all 40 as terminal. The user sees '40 drops can't sync from this account connection' and an xmark on every row, forever. They tap 'Send the magic link' on one: the sheet shows 'This drop can't upload from this account connection' and fires a background retry (ShareDropSheet.swift:189) that is guaranteed to fail identically. They tap again — same. There is no re-own action anywhere in the app, so the honest answer to 'what can the user do' is 'delete them', and the code comments at DropStore.swift:447-450 and ShareDropSheet.swift:182-185 assert a recovery that does not exist. (Real account linking is the SIWA residual and is out of scope per D5; what is in scope is that round 6 shipped a no-op dressed as the fix.)
findings.proposedFix: Make revalidation conditional on the input that actually decides. Give `DropLibrary` the current uid — `func accountDidChange(newUid: String?)` called from RootView.swift:161 with `account.uid` — and re-enqueue only ids whose `drop.ownerUid == newUid`, so a launch after a migration does zero work and zero writes. In ShareDropSheet.sendLink, drop the `library.retrySync(sharedDrop)` call at :189 (it cannot succeed and it would upload unpersisted state) and replace the dead-end copy with the one action that exists: offer to remove the drop, or state plainly that it belongs to a previous connection and cannot be sent from this device.

testCase.name: testAccountChangeRevalidatesOnlyDropsWhoseOwnerMatchesTheNewUid
testCase.steps: Configure `await cloud.setFailSave(DropStoreError.ownedByAnotherAccount, for: stale.id)`; add `stale` and let it go terminal; record `let before = await cloud.saveAttempts`. Call `library.accountDidChange(newUid: "a-different-uid")` and assert `await cloud.saveAttempts == before` — no attempt is spent on a drop whose owner still cannot match — while `terminalSyncFailureIDs.contains(stale.id)` stays true and `pendingSyncIDs` is untouched (today's code spends an attempt and briefly marks it pending). Then set the drop's `ownerUid` to `"matching-uid"`, clear the save failure, call `accountDidChange(newUid: "matching-uid")`, and assert exactly one new attempt and that the verdict clears on the ack.
testCase.infrastructure: None new — GatedCloudStore already exposes `setFailSave(_:for:)` (now `Error?`) and `saveAttempts`. The only production change the test needs is the `newUid` parameter on `accountDidChange`, which is the fix itself.

findings.claim: Two independent round-6 changes compose into a false all-clear: `uploadingCount` excludes pending ids whose rows no longer exist, and the corruption banner is now dismissable. After a whole-file quarantine the Profile confidently reports 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops' for drops that were never uploaded and are now gone, and one tap on Dismiss removes the last trace anywhere in the app.
findings.evidence: `uploadingCount` counts only pending ids that still have a loadable row (DropStore.swift:335-337) and ProfileScreen.swift:92 now branches on it instead of `pendingSyncIDs.count`. After a whole-file quarantine (DropStore.swift:167-177) the local rows are gone, so those pending ids contribute 0 — and the ladder falls straight through to 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops' (:104-108), because `terminalSyncFailureIDs` is empty and a successful cloud read leaves `lastSyncError` nil (:384). The orphan reap that would at least clean the outbox is correctly skipped, since the outcome is `.quarantinedWholeFile`, not `.clean` (:419) — so the ghosts persist in UserDefaults indefinitely. The only remaining signal is the Sent-tab banner, which round 6 made dismissable (DropsListScreen.swift:66 -> DropStore.swift:436-445, which deletes the journal file at :209). Round 4 was stuck but honest here: it rendered 'Uploading N drops…' from the raw `pendingSyncIDs.count`, which at least never claimed the server had them.
findings.failureScenario: A crash mid-write or a disk-full event leaves drops.json unparseable. The user had 3 drops created in the field that had never been uploaded (offline), so their ids are in the persisted outbox. Next launch: the file is quarantined, the library repopulates from the cloud with only the previously-uploaded drops, and the Sent tab shows 'Your saved drops couldn't be read — a backup was kept on this device'. The user taps Dismiss. From that moment the Profile says 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops' with a checkmark, three drops are permanently lost, three ids sit invisibly in the outbox, and no surface in the app indicates anything ever went wrong. The user's mental model — the one the whole 'Synced means the server confirmed it' doctrine was built to protect (ProfileScreen.swift:71-73) — is now actively false.
findings.proposedFix: Two parts. (1) Do not let the discrepancy vanish: when `pendingSyncIDs.count > uploadingCount`, the difference is unaccounted-for work, so the ladder must render a distinct state ('N drops couldn't be found on this device') rather than falling through to Synced — and 'Synced' should require `pendingSyncIDs.isEmpty`, not `uploadingCount == 0`. (2) Hoist the ladder itself: ProfileScreen.swift:74-111 and DropsListScreen.swift:39-69 each recompute status from the raw published sets, which is how they drifted apart; expose one `var syncStatus: SyncStatus` on DropLibrary so there is a single testable definition of 'Synced'. Also consider scoping the Dismiss button to acknowledging the banner while leaving the unresolved-work state intact.

testCase.name: testAQuarantinedLibraryWithAnUnaccountedOutboxNeverReportsSynced
testCase.steps: Seed the injected defaults with `pendingSyncDropIDs = [ghost]`; write unparseable bytes to a temp URL; build `DropLibrary(localStore: LocalDropStore(fileURL: url), cloudStore: nil, defaults: defaults)`; `await library.refresh(near: nil)`. Assert `library.pendingSyncIDs.contains(ghost)` (the reap correctly did not run), `library.uploadingCount == 0`, and — the assertion that fails today — `library.syncStatus != .synced`, expecting `.unaccounted(1)`. Then call `library.acknowledgeReadIncident()`, await it, and assert `library.syncStatus` is STILL not `.synced`, pinning that dismissing the banner cannot manufacture an all-clear.
testCase.infrastructure: Needs the `SyncStatus` enum + `var syncStatus` hoisted onto DropLibrary (the fix). Everything else — `makeDefaults`, `LocalDropStore(fileURL:)`, a nil cloud store — already exists in DropStoreTests.swift:159-175.

additionalTests.name: testIncidentAcknowledgementIsDurableAndDoesNotResurrect
additionalTests.pins: Round 6 claim (5)'s 'incident acknowledgment (user-dismissable banner)' and 'no raw filenames in user copy' — both are implemented (DropStore.swift:176, :187-190, :436-445; DropsListScreen.swift:66) and both have ZERO executing tests. The existing LocalDropStoreTests only pin that the incident SURVIVES loads (DropStoreTests.swift:69-87); nothing pins that a user can end it, that ending it is durable across a subsequent load, or that the copy shown to the user contains no quarantine filename. It also guards the generation race at DropStore.swift:441 that can silently swallow the dismissal.
additionalTests.steps: Write unparseable bytes to a temp URL; `let store = LocalDropStore(fileURL: url)`; build `DropLibrary(localStore: store, cloudStore: nil, defaults: makeDefaults())`; `await library.refresh(near: nil)`. Assert `library.localReadWarning != nil` and — pinning the no-filename claim — `XCTAssertFalse(library.localReadWarning!.contains("corrupt-"))` and that it contains no substring of `url.lastPathComponent`. Call `library.acknowledgeReadIncident()`, then `try await waitUntil { library.localReadWarning == nil }` (the existing helper at DropStoreTests.swift:177). Assert the `.incident` sidecar file no longer exists on disk. Then `await library.refresh(near: nil)` a second time — the store file is now absent, so this exercises the `.absentFile` path — and assert `library.localReadWarning` is still nil, i.e. the acknowledged incident does not resurrect. Finally add a variant that calls `acknowledgeReadIncident()` and immediately `try await library.add(GeoDrop())` in the same turn, then asserts the banner is nil after the next refresh, pinning that the generation guard cannot strand a dismissed banner.
additionalTests.infrastructure: None. Uses `LocalDropStore(fileURL:)`, the existing `makeDefaults()`/`waitUntil` helpers, and a nil cloud store — all already in DropStoreTests.swift.

additionalTests.name: testFirestoreAckedIsBoundedCancellableAndThreeValued
additionalTests.pins: Round 6's headline claim (1) in full: 10 s deadline, encode-throw = rejected, cancellation = queuedLocally, no task parks forever. FirestoreAcked.swift is executed by zero of the 76 passing tests, so every one of those four properties is currently asserted only by the diff's prose. This is also the only way to catch the live contract violation traced in soundAreas — under caller cancellation the ack child falls through `for try await _ in ack` to `return .acked` (FirestoreAcked.swift:82-83) and can win the group, so a cancelled write can report a SERVER ACK instead of the documented `.queuedLocally` (:74-75, :93).
additionalTests.steps: Against the extracted seam: (a) a stream that never yields with `timeout: 0.05` must return `.queuedLocally` and must return within ~0.1 s (bounds the deadline and proves nothing parks); (b) a stream whose continuation yields once must return `.acked`; (c) a stream that calls `finish(throwing: NSError(domain: "test", code: 7))` must return `.rejected` with that error preserved; (d) THE FAILING CASE — wrap the call in `let t = Task { await FirestoreAcked.race(silentStream, timeout: 10) }`, `t.cancel()` before anything yields, and assert `await t.value` is `.queuedLocally`; today this can return `.acked`; (e) drive `setData` with a value whose `encode(to:)` throws and assert it returns `.rejected` essentially immediately rather than after the 10 s deadline, pinning that a staging failure is never mistaken for a queued write.
additionalTests.infrastructure: One seam change: `race(_:timeout:)` is `private static` (FirestoreAcked.swift:76) and `setData`/`delete` take a concrete `DocumentReference`, so nothing is reachable from tests today. Make `race` internal (`@testable import` then reaches it) for cases (a)-(d), and for case (e) add an injectable staging closure — `static func setData<T: Encodable>(_ register: (@escaping (Error?) -> Void) throws -> Void, ackTimeout:)` with the DocumentReference overload calling it — so the Firestore completion can be driven by hand. No Firestore instance, no emulator.

solutions.findingRef: seam-1 (FirestoreAcked.swift:83 — cancellation resolves to .acked)
solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED on mechanism; ONE SUB-CLAIM OVERSTATED. The platform fact is exactly right and is the single most load-bearing piece of documented behaviour in this round: AsyncThrowingStream's iterator returns nil on task cancellation, it does not throw CancellationError. Swift core-team member Franz Busch, on the record: 'Returning nil on cancellation is a totally valid thing for AsyncSequences to do. In fact it is the only thing for AsyncThrowingStream to do since the stream's Failure type might be a specific error so it can't just throw a CancellationError.' So `for try await _ in ack` (FirestoreAcked.swift:82) exits normally under cancellation and falls into `return .acked` at :83, whose comment asserts a false invariant. OVERSTATED: 'the ack child is added first and is resumed first by cancellation propagation, so it beats the sleep child's CancellationError.' ThrowingTaskGroup.next() returns results in COMPLETION order, and cancellation resumes both children; which one lands first is genuinely a race, so the fabricated ack is nondeterministic, not certain — and correspondingly `catch is CancellationError` at :93 is ~half-dead, not 'largely unreachable'. I re-verified the blast radius independently and agree with the reviewer's own conclusion: zero reachable harm today. The only two cancellation sites are enqueueCloudSync (:592) and remove (:524), both of which bump syncGenerations first, and performCloudSync re-checks at :602/:608/:621/:626. AccountService's seedTask is never cancelled (attach(uid:) at :38 does not cancel it), updateProfile's Task (:130) and ReactionOverlay's Task (:185) are unstructured and unowned. So: real latent defect, correct severity for a seam whose whole purpose is not lying, non-blocking today.

solutions.findingRef: seam-2 / state-1 / flows-1 (DropStore.swift:376/:402 — tombstone retirement on a cache-served read)
solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, unanimously and correctly, by three independent lenses. This is the strongest finding of the round and the platform facts are documented, not inferred. Firestore: 'if you get a document while the device is offline, Cloud Firestore returns data from the cache' — a default-source getDocuments() offline SUCCEEDS rather than throwing, and the snapshot carries `metadata.isFromCache == true`. Latency compensation means the local cache has already applied the app's own pending delete. DropStore.swift:376 sets `cloudReadSucceeded = true` on any non-throwing return, FirebaseDropStore.swift:32-34 uses the default source and never reads metadata, and :402-412 then clears both durable id sets and `deleteAttempts` — BEFORE reconcileCloud() at :431, so the replay never fires. The retirement is therefore satisfied by the app's own unacknowledged write. I confirmed the aggravating detail flows-2 raises: `launchCloudDelete` synthesises `var ghost = GeoDrop(); ghost.id = id` (:634-635) with `ownerUid == nil`, so FirebaseDropStore.delete's owner backstop (:95) never fires. Frequency claim ('every offline delete followed by any refresh') is correct — refresh is called from MapScreen.swift:106, DropsListScreen.swift:26 and RootView.swift:157. Note also the known SDK issue that a persisted offline mutation queue does not always resume flushing after a device reboot until new activity occurs, which undercuts the implicit fallback ('Firestore's queue will handle it') that makes discarding the tombstone feel survivable.
solutions.industrialSolution:
Retirement of a delete intent must key on a POSITIVE acknowledgement, never on inference from a read. Two layers:

(1) Correct signal, already used correctly one file away. The codebase's own rule at AccountService.swift:58-61 — `!snapshot.metadata.isFromCache` with the comment 'only a SERVER-confirmed absence means first run' — is the industrial standard and was simply not applied on the drops path. Minimum: propagate provenance through the seam and gate :402 on `cloudReadSucceeded && !readWasFromCache`.

(2) Better, and what I'd actually ship: stop using a set-difference over a query as evidence at all. Add `func confirmDeleted(_ id: UUID) async throws -> Bool` to the cloud seam, implemented as `document(id).getDocument(source: .server)` returning `!snapshot.exists`, called ONLY for ids already in a tombstone set and only when a retirement is being considered (bounded by tombstone count, not library size). `Source.server` throwing `unavailable` while offline is the correct behaviour — retirement must not happen offline. Keep the merge path on the cache-tolerant read so offline refreshes still render. This one change also closes the owner-scoping hole (state-2/flows-2) and the lossy-decode hole I raise in the cross-cutting section, which a provenance flag alone does not.

(3) Belt-and-braces the reviewers agree on and I endorse: require `deleteTasks[id] == nil` so retirement can never race an in-flight delete.

Architecturally: the one signal that genuinely proves the intent satisfied already exists and is being thrown away — `FirestoreAcked.delete` returning `.acked` (FirebaseDropStore.swift:100). Everything at :402-412 is a workaround for having discarded the late verdict (see seam-4). Fixing the late-ack path is the structural version of this fix.

solutions.findingRef: seam-3 / ux-2 / flows-3 (web/firestore.rules:58 — emoji allow-list drift)
solutions.verdictOnFinding:
CONFIRMED, and I re-derived it from the file bytes rather than trusting any lens. Extracting both literals programmatically: app = ❤️ e29da4efb88f, 😂 f09f9882, 🥹 f09fa5b9, 🤯 f09fa4af (ReactionSession.swift:21); rules = ❤️ e29da4efb88f, 🎉 f09f8e89, 😭 f09f98ad, 🤯 f09fa4af, 🥹 f09fa5b9 (firestore.rules:58). App-only: 😂. Rules-only: 🎉, 😭. ❤️ carries the identical U+2764 U+FE0F byte sequence in both files, so the variation-selector hazard the lenses flag is real as a class but not live today. ReactionSessionTests reaches for '🎉' at :29 and :55 — an emoji the bar cannot produce — so the round-6 suite is structurally incapable of detecting the drift. All three lenses are right.

I ESCALATE THE SCOPE. Every lens frames Wave A as 'deploy breaks one of four buttons.' Reading the committed rules against the client, the deploy is a breaking change on THREE axes, and the emoji is the least severe:
(a) rules:60-61 gates `reactions/create` on `get(drops/$(dropId)).data.visibility in ['link','public']`. A sender who shares while offline has `visibility = "link"` only as a locally queued mutation (ShareDropSheet.swift:175 → library.update → queued setData); the SERVER doc still says 'private'. Every reaction to that drop is denied, for 100% of taps, not 25% — and it costs one billed document read per reaction write (Firebase documents that get()/exists() in rules bill a read even when the rule rejects).
(b) rules:40 `allow get: if isOwner() || (signedIn() && linkVisible())` dereferences `resource.data` on both sides. Firebase's guidance is explicit that touching a field on a null resource denies rather than evaluating false; the documented safe forms are `resource.data != null && …` or `exists()`. So a get of a MISSING doc now returns PERMISSION_DENIED instead of a snapshot with `exists == false`, and DropSharingService.fetchSharedDrop's `guard snapshot.exists` (:51) becomes a throw. Same recipient-visible outcome by luck, different code path, and it silently converts 'not found' into 'permission problem' in every log you'll read on deploy day.
(c) rules:55 `allow read: if signedIn()` on reactions is the one collection that did not get the get/list split the parent got — any signed-in user can still enumerate any drop's reactions including `byName`, which contradicts the file's own privacy rationale at :14-15.
solutions.industrialSolution:
Immediately, before any deploy: set rules:58 to exactly the app's four, ['❤️','😂','🥹','🤯'], normalised to the same variation-selector form. Then remove the drift surface permanently — the allow-list buys almost nothing (any signed-in user can already write a permitted emoji) and costs a shipped-product outage. Replace content validation with shape validation, which is the standard rules practice: `request.resource.data.emoji is string && request.resource.data.emoji.size() <= 8`. Keep `keys().hasOnly([...])` — that one genuinely constrains the document and I verified it matches DropReaction's five encoded properties exactly (ReactionService.swift:10-16).

Make drift structurally impossible rather than policed: add `@firebase/rules-unit-testing` against the emulator to CI, driven by the SAME fixture list the client ships, and assert `Set(ReactionSession.reactions)` is accepted and a control string is rejected. That is the documented, supported way to test rules and it is a Wave A gate the repo has already written down but not wired (firebase.json has no `emulators` block).

For (a): either relax the parent-visibility precondition to `resource == null || resource.data.visibility in ['link','public']`-style tolerance, or — better — accept that a reaction to an unpublished parent is a legitimate offline state and drop the precondition, keeping `hasOnly` + `uid == request.auth.uid` as the real guard. For (b): rewrite as `allow get: if signedIn() && (resource == null || resource.data.ownerUid == request.auth.uid || resource.data.visibility in ['link','public'])` so a missing document reads as not-found rather than denied. For (c): split reactions read into get/list and scope list to the drop owner and the reacting uid.

Deploy mechanics, verified against the repo: web/firebase.json has a `firestore.rules` block but no `firestore.indexes.json` and no `emulators` block, so `firebase deploy --only firestore` will prompt or fail on indexes. `firebase deploy --only firestore:rules` is the working invocation for the Wave A gate.

solutions.findingRef: seam-4 (FirestoreAcked.swift:28 — .queuedLocally is terminal, no late-ack re-check)
solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED as a defect; the reviewer's FIX is the wrong one of the two it proposes, and one sub-claim is overstated. The gap is real and self-documented: FirestoreAcked.swift:27-28 promises 'callers keep their pending state and retry the ACK check later, not the write,' and no caller implements an ack re-check. I verified the two durable surfaces: AccountService.updateProfile sets `statusText = "Profile saved on this device — syncing when online"` (:138) and the profile listener (:46-72) writes `profile` but never touches `statusText`, so the only clear is another profile edit — an online user is told they are offline, indefinitely. ReactionSession's queued pill (:231) has no correction path at all, though the ux lens is right that its lifetime is bounded (~5 s, ack deadline 10 s at FirestoreAcked.swift:29 vs wrap 15 s at ReactionSession.swift:60) and I accept that as tolerable. OVERSTATED: 'recovery requires switching to the Map tab, which re-uploads the whole document and — on the same congested network — times out again, producing a re-write loop that costs bandwidth on exactly the connection that is already saturated.' Firestore coalesces pending mutations for the same document in the local queue; a repeated identical setData is not N payloads on the wire. The waste is real (a Task + a UserDefaults write per pass) but it is not a bandwidth amplifier. Severity MEDIUM is right.
solutions.industrialSolution:
Do not invent a `lateAck` Task handle — that adds an unstructured lifetime to the one seam whose charter is bounded, cancellable writes. Firestore already publishes the exact signal, and it is the canonical answer to 'did my queued write commit?': listen with metadata changes and read `snapshot.metadata.hasPendingWrites`. Firebase's own documentation states that a listener opted into metadata updates 'will receive another snapshot with hasPendingWrites equal to false once the writes have been committed to the backend'. Zero extra writes, zero extra reads beyond the listener you already pay for.

Per-surface, cheapest first:
(1) AccountService — one line. The profile listener at :46 ALREADY passes `includeMetadataChanges: true`. Add `if !snapshot.metadata.hasPendingWrites { self.statusText = nil }` inside the callback. That closes the stuck 'you are offline' string completely and costs nothing.
(2) DropLibrary — do not make reconcileCloud re-`setData` an `ackTimedOut` id. Replace the re-push with a metadata observation on the drop document. This is the recorded listener-diff end-state target, so the fix composes with the roadmap instead of competing with it: once drops are observed rather than polled, `pendingSyncIDs` clears from `hasPendingWrites == false` and the whole reconcile loop shrinks.
(3) ReactionSession — leave as is. The pill under-claims for ~5 s and then disappears; under-claiming is the correct direction for a truth surface and the cost of fixing it exceeds the harm.

solutions.findingRef: seam-5 / state-5 / ux-5 (ShareDropSheet.swift:189 — retrySync(sharedDrop) pushes unpersisted state)
solutions.verdictOnFinding:
CONFIRMED by three lenses, and it is the cheapest high-value fix in the round — one identifier. Verified end to end: `sharedDrop` (ShareDropSheet.swift:173-178) applies `visibility = "link"` and `recipientName`; the refusal branch (:186-191) calls `library.retrySync(sharedDrop)`; `retrySync` (DropStore.swift:462-464) forwards straight to `enqueueCloudSync`, which touches neither `drops` nor `local.save` — only `cloud.save` at :607, which writes `visibility: "link"` (FirebaseDropStore.swift:61-68). The success path two lines down does the opposite and correctly persists first via `library.update(sharedDrop)` (:195). GeoDrop.visibility defaults to 'private' (GeoDrop.swift:64), so the local row keeps saying private. The consequences all three lenses list are correct; I additionally confirmed seam-5's reaction-listener consequence, which is the most damaging and which the other two lenses missed: `ReactionService.watchedDrops` (:75-83) filters the LOCAL array on `visibility != "private"`, so `listenKey` (:91-96) omits the drop and RootView's `.task(id:)` (:148) never subscribes — the sender's toast, the loop's entire payoff, is structurally dead for that drop.

THE LENSES DISAGREE ON THE FIX AND ONE OF THEM IS WRONG. state-5 and ux-5 say `retrySync(drop)`; seam-5 prefers `Task { try? await library.update(sharedDrop) }` because 'it matches what the user just asked for.' seam-5's preference is wrong against the charter: `update(sharedDrop)` persists AND publishes the share the app has just told the user in red that it cannot do. That converts a background contradiction into a foreground one. state-5/ux-5 are right.
solutions.industrialSolution:
Change ShareDropSheet.swift:189 to `library.retrySync(drop)` — revalidate the row as stored. Then close the seam rather than the instance, which is the ux-5 recommendation and the correct engineering answer: replace `retrySync(_ drop: GeoDrop)` (DropStore.swift:462-464) with `revalidateTerminal(_ id: UUID)` that looks its own row up in `drops`. This is the standard 'a server-authority operation must not accept caller-supplied state' rule — the same rule that makes `launchCloudDelete`'s synthesised ghost (:634) a mistake. After the change no caller can push an unpersisted mutation through the revalidation path, and the fix is unit-testable without a UI test.

Land this together with the flows-5 fix. With flows-5 uncorrected the revalidation cannot succeed anyway, so fixing seam-5 alone yields a correct no-op wearing the costume of a recovery action.

Secondary, worth taking in the same edit (the ux lens noted it and declined a slot; I agree it is small but it is two lines): `shareError` is `@State` and is never cleared when a background revalidation succeeds, so the sheet keeps showing the refusal after the verdict has cleared. Clear it in an `.onChange(of: library.terminalSyncFailureIDs)`.

solutions.findingRef: seam-6 (FirebaseDropStore.swift:104 — the notFound delete branch is dead in both rule worlds)
solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, with primary-source backing the reviewer asserted but did not cite. Firestore delete is documented as succeeding on an absent document: the Node Firestore reference states plainly that 'a delete for a non-existing document is treated as a success (unless lastUpdateTime is provided)', and the REST v1 API exposes a `currentDocument` precondition with `exists: true` precisely BECAUSE an unconditional delete of a missing document otherwise succeeds. So under the committed v3 rules (`allow delete: if signedIn() && (resource == null || resource.data.ownerUid == request.auth.uid)`, rules:51-52) the server acks and control leaves at FirebaseDropStore.swift:101, never reaching `.notFound` at :104-112. Under the deployed v2 rules the same delete is PERMISSION_DENIED, which also does not match the `where` clause. Dead in both worlds; the comment at :107-111 relabelled the folklore instead of removing it. LOW is the right severity for the comment, but I endorse the reviewer's point that the LIVE harm it conceals is not low: on v2, deleting a never-uploaded drop burns all three `deleteAttempts` (:652-659) and lands a permanent `unresolvedDeleteIDs` entry for an intent that was satisfied by construction — and finding state-1 then retires it on the first cache-served read, so the two defects mask each other and neither shows up in the logs as what it is.

solutions.findingRef: state-2 / flows-2 (DropStore.swift:403/:408 — retirement against a uid-scoped query)
solutions.verdictOnFinding:
CONFIRMED, and it is a genuinely DIFFERENT mechanism from state-1, not a duplicate — the flows lens is right to insist on that (D4). It fires even when every read is server-confirmed, because `cloudIDs` derives from `.whereField("ownerUid", isEqualTo: uid)` (FirebaseDropStore.swift:33): absence means 'not owned by the reading account', never 'not there'. Under a fresh uid the predicate is true for EVERY id the user ever created, and :403/:408 clear both durable sets from UserDefaults in a single pass (:692-695, :702-705). The platform fact is documented: Firebase's anonymous-auth guidance states users 'will be assigned a new user ID every time they sign in to the app on a new device' — the anonymous uid lives in the keychain and is not carried across a device migration, while the app container (and its UserDefaults) IS restored from backup. So the tombstones outlive exactly the identity that could have honoured them, and round 6 then destroys them.

flows-2 adds the aggravating factor that state-2 understates and I verified: round 6 made the give-up DURABLE. `deleteAttempts` is in-memory (:298), but after three refusals the id migrates to the persisted `unresolvedDeleteIDs` (:655-659), and `reconcileCloud` replays only `pendingDeleteIDs` (:568). In rounds 4/5 every relaunch bought three fresh attempts; from round 6 the delete is never retried again on any future launch. HIGH is correct for both.

I RAISE ITS PRIORITY ABOVE ITS RATING for one reason the state lens flagged and I endorse: this is the only finding that makes a recorded end-state target strictly HARDER rather than merely unaddressed. SIWA account-linking is the sole mechanism that could ever honour these intents; round 6 destroys them before it lands, so by the time linking ships there is nothing left to replay.
solutions.industrialSolution:
Stamp every durable intent with the principal that issued it and never resolve it under a different principal. This is standard practice for any client-side outbox that can outlive an identity (it is the same reason durable job queues carry a tenant id):

    private var pendingDeleteOwnerUid: [UUID: String]   // persisted alongside the id sets

Pass the reading account into refresh — `refresh(near:as uid:)`, or inject a `uidProvider` into DropLibrary — and run BOTH retirement loops only for tombstones whose stamped uid equals the reading uid. Leave every other tombstone durable and suppressing, untouched. Combined with the state-1/flows-1 fix the predicate finally states something true: 'the same account got a server-confirmed, per-document check that this id is absent.'

Second change, which flows-2 gets right and the other lenses miss: stop synthesising the owner-less ghost at :634-635. Carry the recorded ownerUid into the delete so `FirebaseDropStore.delete`'s backstop (:95) can recognise 'this document belongs to a previous connection and cannot be deleted from here' and SURFACE it, instead of firing three anonymous requests the server was always going to refuse. That converts three silent refusals into one honest, actionable state — which is the charter.

Third, and this is where the residual ledger points: `unresolvedDeleteIDs` stamped with its issuing uid is precisely the replay ledger SIWA linking will consume. Treat it as an asset to preserve, not garbage to collect.

solutions.findingRef: state-3 (DropStore.swift:625 — terminal verdicts have one client-side producer that cannot fire)
solutions.verdictOnFinding:
CONFIRMED, and in my judgement this is the MOST UNDER-RATED finding in the entire set — it should outrank several of the CRITICALs. I re-derived every step rather than trusting the lens. `DropStoreError.ownedByAnotherAccount` is thrown at exactly one place, FirebaseDropStore.swift:55-57, from the purely local `if let owner = drop.ownerUid, owner != uid`. `stored.ownerUid = uid` at :59 mutates only the cloud-bound copy; the library never writes ownerUid back, so drops.json never receives it. The only two producers of a non-nil ownerUid into `DropLibrary.drops` are (a) the uid-scoped cloud read, where owner == uid by construction so the check can never fire, and (b) `DropSharingService.fetchSharedDrop` (:54-55), which also sets `receivedViaLink = true` and is filtered out at DropStore.swift:583 before reaching save. Conclusion: for the ordinary drop, ownerUid is nil and the ONLY producer of terminality cannot fire.

That means the entire terminal apparatus — `terminalSyncFailureIDs`, its durable UserDefaults key, the ProfileScreen branch (:78-87), the DropsListScreen banner (:39-47), the per-row xmark (:92-96, :154-159), the ShareDropSheet refusal (:135-143, :186-191), the accountDidChange revalidation, and four of the eight round-6 tests — is decoration in the field. Every REAL server refusal lands in the generic catch at DropStore.swift:625-628, keeps the drop in `pendingSyncIDs` forever, is re-pushed by reconcileCloud (:563) on every refresh, renders no badge, and reaches ShareDropSheet's caption ladder at :144-150 as 'Still uploading — the link starts working once your drop reaches the cloud.' `sendLink()` then sees an empty `terminalSyncFailureIDs`, skips the refusal, and hands out the link.

Two additions of my own. First: the committed rules v3 make this worse on deploy day, because `allow update: if isOwner() && request.resource.data.ownerUid == resource.data.ownerUid` (rules:46-47) is precisely the rule that will start returning PERMISSION_DENIED — so Wave A converts this from a migration-only path into a routine one. Second: the generic catch retries forever, so a permanently-denied write becomes an unbounded re-push loop across every affected drop on every Map-tab appear; with App Check enforcement (a normal Wave A step) that is every drop in the library.

solutions.findingRef: state-4 / ux-4 / flows-6 (DropStore.swift:335, ProfileScreen.swift:92/:105 — uploadingCount lets the ladder fall through to 'Synced')
solutions.verdictOnFinding:
MECHANISM CONFIRMED; state-4's HEADLINE FAILURE SCENARIO IS WRONG ON A PLATFORM FACT, and correcting it makes the finding MORE frequent, not less. The mechanism is exactly as described: `uploadingCount` (DropStore.swift:335-337) filters `pendingSyncIDs` to ids present in `drops`; `DropLibrary.init` restores pendingSyncIDs from UserDefaults (:322-329) but never loads `drops`; refresh's local-failure branch (:352-360) returns before `drops` is assigned; ProfileScreen.swift:92 branches on `uploadingCount > 0` and the terminal `else` at :104-108 prints 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops'. The ladder consults neither pendingSyncIDs, nor unresolvedDeleteIDs, nor localReadWarning. Round 4's `!library.pendingSyncIDs.isEmpty` branch was over-optimistic but never claimed server confirmation, so this IS a round-6 regression.

WRONG: state-4's trigger — 'the app is launched into the background by a location or push event while the device is still locked, so drops.json is unreadable under NSFileProtectionComplete.' I checked. Config/Info.plist declares no `UIBackgroundModes`; there is no significant-location monitoring, no push entitlement, and the app never sets a protection class, so files inherit `NSFileProtectionCompleteUntilFirstUserAuthentication` — accessible from the first unlock after boot and thereafter even when locked (Apple DTS, Quinn 'The Eskimo!'). This app cannot be launched at all before first unlock. The scenario is unreachable.

The REACHABLE paths are the ones ux-4 and flows-6 give, and one neither of them names: (a) the local-read abort at :352-360, which leaves `drops` empty for the whole session; (b) the whole-file quarantine composition (flows-6, correct); (c) EVERY COLD LAUNCH — `AccountService.start()` attaches synchronously when a keychain user exists (:22-24), so `account.uid` is non-nil immediately, the ladder skips 'Connecting…' (:74), and renders 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops' for the entire duration of the first refresh, before a single byte has been read. flows-6's composition claim (quarantine + dismissable banner + uploadingCount ⇒ no trace anywhere) is correct and is the most damaging framing of the three.
solutions.industrialSolution:
Two structural changes; the second is what stops this class recurring.

(1) 'Synced' must be the negation of every failure state, never a fallthrough `else`. Define one exhaustive status on the model and render it everywhere:

    enum SyncStatus { case connecting, notLoadedYet, readError(String), terminalFailures(Int), unresolvedDeletes(Int), notUploadable(Int), uploading(Int), synced }
    var syncStatus: SyncStatus  // on DropLibrary

with `.synced` requiring `pendingSyncIDs.isEmpty && terminalSyncFailureIDs.isEmpty && unresolvedDeleteIDs.isEmpty && localReadWarning == nil && lastSyncError == nil && hasCompletedFirstRefresh`. When `pendingSyncIDs.count > uploadingCount`, the difference is unaccounted-for work and gets its own honest branch ('N drops couldn't be found on this device'), which is what flows-6's fix (1) asks for and is correct.

(2) Add `hasCompletedFirstRefresh` and render `.connecting`/`.notLoadedYet` until it flips. 'Unknown is not healthy' is the discipline AccountService already follows correctly at :59; the drops path needs the same. This alone closes the every-cold-launch path.

(3) Hoist the ladder, per flows-6: ProfileScreen.swift:74-111 and DropsListScreen.swift:39-69 each recompute status from raw published sets, which is exactly how they drifted. One computed property, one definition of 'Synced', unit-testable with no UI test. Render `localReadWarning` on the Profile too — Profile is where users go to ask 'are my drops safe', and it is currently the one surface that cannot answer.

solutions.findingRef: state-6 (DropStore.swift:490 — redemption writes receivedViaLink to disk, making delete nondeterministic)
solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, and I verified the nondeterminism mechanism myself because it is the part that makes the finding serious rather than cosmetic. `RootView.swift:63` persists the fetched copy via `library.update(drop, persist: true)`, and `receivedViaLink` is a real encoded/decoded key (GeoDrop.swift:125), so `true` lands in drops.json. `remove()` then takes the viewer early-return at :531 BEFORE `markPendingDelete`/`launchCloudDelete`, and `enqueueCloudSync` bails at :583 for the same reason. Now the timing: a re-received OWN drop is NOT placed in `pendingSyncIDs` (enqueueCloudSync returns before markPending), so the cloud-merge guard at :381 (`if pendingSyncIDs.contains(drop.id), merged[drop.id] != nil { continue }`) does not protect it — the cloud copy, whose `receivedViaLink` was stripped at FirebaseDropStore.swift:60, overwrites the in-memory row at :382. Disk says true, memory says nil, and which one `remove()` reads depends purely on whether a cloud read has landed this session. Same user, same gesture, opposite outcomes. HomeScreen.swift:54/:60 partitions the UI on the same unstable flag, so the drop also migrates between sections across refreshes. MEDIUM is defensible; I would call it HIGH given that the losing branch leaves a link-readable document alive with no tombstone, no banner and no retry.
solutions.industrialSolution:
Do not overload a provenance flag as an authorization flag — that is the root error, and it is a recurring one in this codebase (the same conflation is why `FirebaseDropStore.save` strips the flag at :60 and why `watchedDrops` has to test it at :78-80). Separate the two concepts in the model:
- `receivedViaLink: Bool?` — transient PRESENTATION provenance ('this arrived through a link this session'), never persisted, never consulted for a write decision.
- ownership — durable, derived from `ownerUid` compared against the current uid.

Then gate the viewer early-returns at :531 and :583 on ownership: `drop.ownerUid != nil && drop.ownerUid != currentUid`. Note the dependency the reviewer does not flag: that predicate needs a reliably persisted ownerUid, which per state-3 does not exist today. These two must ship together, or the new gate is as unreachable as the old one.

Interim one-liner to take immediately, inside the redemption block at :490-494: clear `receivedViaLink` before persisting when the fetched `ownerUid` equals the current uid, so the user's own drop is never written to disk as a viewer copy.

Also harden the redemption itself: it currently fires on ANY received-drop update regardless of whether the id is in either delete set, and it clears `deleteAttempts` too — so the RootView.swift:63 persist that runs on EVERY link open touches delete bookkeeping. Guard it on membership.

solutions.findingRef: ux-1 (MemoryScreen.swift:139 — the payoff screen claims receipt for rejected reactions)
solutions.verdictOnFinding:
CONFIRMED, and I would RAISE it to the top of the non-rules blocking set. It is a direct round-6 regression manufactured by the critical-1 fix: in round 5 `reactionFailed()` did not start the wrap, so a rejected reaction never reached this screen; ReactionSession.swift:59-61 now starts it unconditionally on the tap, and RootView.swift:80-89 constructs MemoryScreen with `myReaction: reactionSession.sentEmoji` and NO delivery value. MemoryScreen.swift:137-142 then synthesizes `DropReaction(emoji: myReaction, uid: "", byName: "")` whenever the cloud fetch at :72 returns empty and renders it as '❤️ ×1 from <them>' (:46-52) beneath 'That made <their> day.' (:40) and above 'Save memory' (:58). Nothing on the screen reads `session.delivery`. The ux lens' timing argument is right and I re-verified it against the real line numbers (its own cites are wrong — see the audit): the ack deadline is 10 s at FirestoreAcked.swift:29, the wrap is 15 s at ReactionSession.swift:60, so `delivery` is ALWAYS settled before the screen appears. This is deterministic, not racy.

I ADD A FREQUENCY CORRECTION THAT MAKES IT WORSE. The lens models the failure as poor signal or an unuploaded parent. The most common path is neither: `ReactionService.send` throws at :46-49 (`guard AppConfig.firebaseConfigured, let uid = Auth.auth().currentUser?.uid`) SYNCHRONOUSLY, before any network. RootView presents ReceiveScreen straight off `.onOpenURL` (:50-73) with no auth gate, so a viewer who opens a magic link on a cold launch — the single most common way this app is ever used by a new person — can tap, get `.failed` in microseconds on a perfect connection, and be handed a confetti receipt 15 seconds later, with a Save-to-Photos button.
solutions.industrialSolution:
Pass `reactionSession.delivery` into MemoryScreen from RootView.swift:80-89 and branch on it. Only `.delivered` may include `myReaction` in the synthesized row at MemoryScreen.swift:139. `.failed` → drop the synthesized row, add an explicit caveat and a retry affordance ('Your ❤️ didn't reach Sam — tap to send it now'). `.queued` → render as pending ('Your ❤️ sends when you're back online'), not as a count. Keep the confetti and the watched-seconds recap — those are honest — and strip only the delivery claim. Gate the `saveToPhotos` copy at :58 so a keepsake of an undelivered reaction does not read as a receipt.

The generalisable rule, and the reason this belongs in the round's retrospective: MemoryScreen.swift:138-140 is a CONFIDENT DEFAULT — when the source of truth returns empty, the code fabricates a plausible record rather than rendering an unknown. That is the same anti-pattern as ProfileScreen's `else`-is-'Synced' (ux-4) and FirestoreAcked's fallthrough-is-`.acked` (seam-1). In a product whose charter is making failure visible, every empty/fallthrough/default branch must resolve to the UNKNOWN state, and the good state must be reached only by positive evidence.

Secondary, cheap and worth taking: add an auth gate before the reaction bar is interactive, or queue the tap until `account.uid` is non-nil — the synchronous `notSignedIn` throw is a self-inflicted rejection that no amount of honest copy makes acceptable.

solutions.findingRef: ux-3 (DropStore.swift:657 — unresolvedDeleteIDs is durable, suppressing, and has zero surface)
solutions.verdictOnFinding:
CONFIRMED; I re-ran the grep myself and `unresolvedDelete` appears in DropStore.swift and nowhere else under AugmentMeReality/. No view reads it. Verified the rest of the chain: :655-659 migrates the id and clears `deleteAttempts`; `reconcileCloud` (:568-571) replays only `pendingDeleteIDs`, so nothing ever retries; :396 suppresses the id from the merged map so the row vanishes from the Sent list; ProfileScreen.swift:92-111 dropped the deletions branch in the same round, so the ladder falls through to 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops.' The lens is right that the round-5 argument ('the user considers a deleted drop deleted') justifies hiding an IN-FLIGHT delete and does not justify hiding a PERMANENTLY REFUSED one, and right that the harm is the surviving remote copy, not local resurrection. The code comment at :646-651 addresses only the local half.

This is round 6 shipping a brand-new durable verdict with no producer test for its surface, no surface, and no control — which is a partial re-creation of the very class round-5 critical 2 named. Critical 2 said 'nothing durable may be unretirable'; round 6 closed that and opened 'nothing durable may be silent'.
solutions.industrialSolution:
Adopt the invariant explicitly and enforce it in review: a durable set that (a) suppresses user-visible content and (b) the app has stopped working on MUST have a surface and a user control. Concretely:
- ProfileScreen ladder: an `unresolvedDeleteIDs` branch ABOVE `.synced` — 'N drop(s) couldn't be removed from the cloud' — and `unresolvedDeleteIDs.isEmpty` becomes a hard precondition of the 'Synced' branch (this falls out of the single `SyncStatus` enum recommended for state-4/ux-4).
- DropsListScreen: the rows are suppressed at :396, so a per-row badge is impossible — it needs its own small 'Couldn't delete' section rendered from the id set, with a Retry that resets `deleteAttempts[id]`, moves the id back to `pendingDeleteIDs` and calls `launchCloudDelete`.
- Keep both retirement paths as built (:402-412 once its predicate is fixed, and :490-494) — the lens is right that the mechanism is correct and the silence is the defect.

Strategic note that changes how this should be prioritised: once state-2's uid stamping lands, `unresolvedDeleteIDs` stops being a bug bucket and becomes the delete-intent replay ledger that SIWA account-linking will consume. Give it a surface and a control now and it is an asset; leave it silent and the linking work will find an empty drawer.

solutions.findingRef: ux-6 (DropStore.swift:441 — acknowledgeReadIncident guards on a generation it does not own)
solutions.verdictOnFinding:
CONFIRMED; both orderings are real and I traced each. `acknowledgeReadIncident` (:436-445) captures `refreshGeneration` at tap and never bumps it, while `refresh` bumps on entry (:343) and `add`/`update`/`remove` bump at :469/:485/:512. Ordering A: a refresh already in flight has read `warning` at :363 BEFORE `acknowledgeIncident()` deleted the journal; its guards at :364/:367 all pass because the acknowledgment never bumped the counter; it re-assigns `localReadWarning = warning` at :365 and the banner returns with nothing to tap. Ordering B: any refresh or mutator starting after the tap makes :441 fail and the visible clear never happens. B is easy to hit — RootView.swift:155-162 fires a refresh on the uid task and DropsListScreen.swift:24-30 puts a refresh button on the very screen the banner lives on.

The detail that raises this above cosmetic, and which the lens states correctly: the journal is deleted FIRST (:439 → :188 → :209), so on ordering B the durable incident record is gone while the banner remains. solutions.findingRef: flows-4 (ReactionService.swift:118 — the sender toast filter swallows late-flushing reactions)
solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, with TWO independent causes, both of which I verified and both of which must be fixed — the lens correctly identifies both but the second is easy to lose in the write-up. Cause 1: `reaction.at > self.startedAt` (:118), where `startedAt = Date()` is stamped once at service construction (:25) and ReactionService is a `@StateObject` per app process (RootView.swift:14). `DropReaction.at` defaults to `Date()` on the VIEWER's device at tap time (:15, constructed at :50-52) and is written unchanged into the queued document, so a reaction stamped at 14:00 and flushed at 18:00 is compared against a sender session that began at 17:00 and discarded. Cause 2: the query is `.order(by: "at", descending: true).limit(to: 1)` (:111), so a late-flushing older reaction is not even in the result set once any newer reaction exists — it can never surface regardless of the timestamp filter. The lens is right that round 6 did not create the filter but does own the broken promise, because ReactionSession.swift:231 turned an ambiguous 'Sending…' into a concrete 'Will send to <sender> when you're back online.' MEDIUM is right as a standalone; it is HIGH in combination with ux-1, because together they mean an offline reaction is invisible to BOTH parties while both are told it worked.
solutions.industrialSolution:
This is a textbook Firestore mistake with a textbook four-part answer:

(1) Never order by a client clock. Write the ordering field with `FieldValue.serverTimestamp()` (keep the client tap time as a separate field if the recap wants it) so ordering reflects COMMIT order, not tap order. The committed rules' `keys().hasOnly(['id','emoji','uid','byName','at'])` (rules:59) still permits this. The client must then tolerate the documented `ServerTimestampBehavior`: a server timestamp reads as null in the local echo until the server commits.

(2) Detect novelty from the LISTENER, not from the payload. Use `snapshot.documentChanges` and toast on `.added` after the first snapshot — this is the documented Firestore idiom for 'a new item arrived' (DocumentChange.type is added/modified/removed, and every document in the initial snapshot arrives as `.added`, so you skip the first callback). Combine with `snapshot.metadata.hasPendingWrites == false` so you never toast your own local echo.

(3) Replace `startedAt`'s job properly: persist a per-drop `lastToastedAt` watermark so a relaunch does not re-toast history. That is what the cutoff was actually for, and it survives process restarts, which `Date()` at construction does not.

(4) Raise `limit(to: 1)`. A batch of reactions flushed together must not collapse to one; take the top N and toast the ones above the watermark.

The lens' suggestion to hoist the decision into a `nonisolated static func shouldToast(...)` beside the existing `watchedDrops`/`listenKey` statics is exactly right and worth doing — those two statics are the one place this codebase already solved the 'two definitions drift apart' problem (counsel PBS-3), and the pattern should be reused rather than reinvented.

solutions.findingRef: flows-5 (DropStore.swift:451 — both revalidation paths are structurally incapable of clearing a verdict)
solutions.verdictOnFinding:
CONFIRMED, and it is the finding that makes state-3 unavoidable rather than merely likely. Verified: a terminal verdict is produced only by `ownedByAnotherAccount` (DropStore.swift:618-624), thrown from `FirebaseDropStore.save`'s purely local `if let owner = drop.ownerUid, owner != uid` (:55-57) with no network involved. `accountDidChange()` (:451-457) and `retrySync` (:462-464) both re-enter that identical comparison with identical inputs — nothing rewrites `drop.ownerUid` locally, since `stored.ownerUid = uid` at :59 mutates only the cloud record. The verdict can flip only if the current uid becomes equal to the drop's original uid, and anonymous uids are keychain-resident and not migrated, so once lost it is gone. Each invocation still performs a real `markPending` + UserDefaults write (:584, :665-667) before failing back.

ONE REFINEMENT the lens does not make, which follows from state-3: because `ownerUid` is nil for the ordinary drop, `terminalSyncFailureIDs` is usually EMPTY, so `accountDidChange()` typically iterates nothing and does no work at all. The '40 drops re-enqueued every launch' scenario requires drops that acquired a non-nil ownerUid — which state-6 shows does happen, via the re-received-own-drop path that writes the fetched ownerUid to disk. So the wasteful-loop harm is real but narrower than stated; the dead-end-affordance harm is universal. The lens' core judgement — 'round 6 shipped a no-op dressed as the fix' — is correct and is the right thing to say.
solutions.industrialSolution:
Two parts, and the second matters more.

(1) Make revalidation conditional on the input that actually decides. Give DropLibrary the uid: `func accountDidChange(newUid: String?)`, called from RootView.swift:161 with `account.uid`, re-enqueuing only ids whose `drop.ownerUid == newUid`. A launch after a migration then does zero work and zero writes. This is the same 'pass the deciding input rather than re-deriving it' correction that state-2 needs for the retirement loops, and both should land in one change.

(2) Never ship a recovery affordance whose success condition is unreachable — it converts a clear dead end into a loop the user blames themselves for, which is the opposite of the charter. Under anonymous-only auth there is no re-own action, so the copy must name the action that EXISTS. Replace ShareDropSheet's `library.retrySync(sharedDrop)` at :189 (per seam-5, with `retrySync(drop)` or better `revalidateTerminal(id)`) and change the message from an implied retry to a statement plus the real option: 'This drop belongs to a previous account connection and can't be sent from this device' with a Remove action. Same for the Profile and Sent banners.

Note the ordering dependency across findings: once state-3's server-side terminal classification lands, revalidation becomes MEANINGFUL for the first time (a rules change, a quota reset or an App Check fix genuinely can flip a PERMISSION_DENIED verdict), so the affordance stops being a lie. Fix state-3 first and flows-5's copy problem largely dissolves; fix flows-5 alone and you have honestly-labelled dead ends.
