solutions.findingRef: AUDIT of sound areas — 'registry ownership is airtight' (seam lens) is overstated; the DELETE pipeline has no generation discipline at all
solutions.verdictOnFinding:
CONCLUSION AGREED, STRENGTH WRONG, AND THE LENS AUDITED THE WRONG PIPELINE. The seam lens says of `performCloudSync`: 'I could not construct a stuck-registry interleaving.' I agree for the SAVE pipeline — the entry guard at :602 precedes the defer at :603-605, but every path that can fail it (enqueueCloudSync :590-592, remove :523-525) bumps `syncGenerations` first and either installs a newer task or nils the slot, and the defer's own `if syncGenerations[id] == generation` prevents a stale task clobbering a fresh one. Verified branch by branch.

What no lens checked: the DELETE pipeline has none of that. Grepping the file, `syncGenerations` guards appear at :602/:604/:608/:621/:626 — there is no `deleteGenerations` anywhere. `launchCloudDelete` (:631-663) has no defer, no entry guard, and no generation; `deleteTasks[id] = nil` is a plain trailing statement at :661. `remove()` calls `launchCloudDelete(id)` at :533 without checking whether `deleteTasks[id]` is already occupied, so a reconcile-launched delete and a remove-launched delete for the same id can both be live with the registry holding only the second, and the first's completion nils the slot for the second — after which `reconcileCloud`'s `deleteTasks[id] == nil` gate (:569) admits a third. `deleteAttempts` is incremented from whichever task loses the race, so the three-strike budget is not reliably three. I could not construct a field-reachable harm today (remove() for an already-tombstoned id is not reachable), so this is not a finding — but 'airtight' is the wrong word for a subsystem where half the pipeline has the discipline and half does not, and the delete half is the one that makes destructive durable decisions.
solutions.industrialSolution: Give the delete pipeline the same generation discipline the save pipeline has: a `deleteGenerations: [UUID: UInt64]` bumped by `remove`/`reconcileCloud`, an entry guard, a `defer` that nils the registry only under the current generation, and a post-await generation re-check before any `clearPendingDelete`/`markUnresolvedDelete` mutation. This is not speculative hardening — the round-4/round-6 save-side guards exist precisely because the same interleaving was a live bug there, and the delete side now carries strictly more durable, strictly more destructive state (`unresolvedDeleteIDs`, the three-strike budget, the retirement path) than the save side did when it was hardened. Symmetric mechanisms should carry symmetric discipline; asymmetry is where the next regression lands.

solutions.findingRef: AUDIT of sound areas — 'VERIFIED SAFE: reactions cannot auto-double-deliver' (seam lens) is right in fact, wrong in tense
solutions.verdictOnFinding: PARTLY WRONG. The seam lens files multi-send under a forward-looking NOTE ('any auto-retry added later WOULD create duplicate reaction documents; that seam is unprotected today'). The unprotected part is not hypothetical: ReactionOverlay's button (:181-197) has no in-flight guard, `didReact` does not cancel the previous send, and `DropReaction.id` is a fresh UUID per call (:11), so N taps write N documents TODAY, in the shipping build. The ux lens caught this and ruled it defensible product semantics ('each tap a reaction'), which I accept as a product call — a 15-second live session producing a reaction stream is coherent, and the sender's per-reaction toast is the payoff. What is NOT defensible, and what the ux lens correctly isolates, is the presentation mismatch: the bar draws an exclusive selection ring that MOVES on each tap (:203-212) and the pill is singular ('Sent to X'), both presenting a replace-my-one-reaction model over an append-only backend, so the viewer systematically under-counts what the sender received. The ux lens also spotted the constraint that makes the obvious fix illegal: a uid-keyed reaction document id (the standard dedup) would be rejected by the committed rules, which set `allow update: if false` (rules:66). The seam lens missed that entirely.
solutions.industrialSolution: Pick a model and make the UI and the rules agree, because right now three layers disagree. If append-only is the product (I think it is — it is the better AR-session semantic), then: drop the exclusive selection ring in favour of a per-emoji count chip, change the pill to a running count ('3 sent to Sam'), and raise the sender-side `limit(to: 1)` (ReactionService.swift:111) so a burst is not collapsed to one toast — that last item is also flows-4's fix, so they land together. If replace-my-one is the product, then the document id must be uid-keyed and `allow update` must permit an author overwriting their own reaction (`request.auth.uid == resource.data.uid`) — a rules change and a client change that MUST ship in the same deploy, or every second tap is denied. Either way, add the in-flight guard so a double-tap is not two documents by accident.

solutions.findingRef: AUDIT of sound areas — the seedProfile 'self-heal' dismissal (seam lens) uses the cache as evidence of server state
solutions.verdictOnFinding: THE DISMISSAL IS INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT WITH THE ROUND'S OWN CRITICAL. The seam lens chases the right concern — that mapping an unanswered seed to `.queuedLocally` collapses round 2's bounded three-attempt retry (AccountService.swift:85-110) to a single attempt — and then dismisses it: 'it self-heals: the pending local mutation makes the cached user doc `exists`, so the listener sets `profile` from it.' That mechanism is real (the listener's `if let snapshot, snapshot.exists` at :49-51 fires on the local echo). But it produces exactly the failure class this round exists to abolish: `self.profile = try snapshot.data(as: UserProfile.self)` latches a profile from a CACHED, server-unacknowledged write, and `seedProfile`'s `.queuedLocally` branch returns at :98-101 without setting `statusText`, so nothing anywhere tells the user their identity has not been established. The lens is using the local cache as evidence of server state — the identical error that state-1/flows-1/seam-2 file as CRITICAL two lenses over, and that AccountService.swift:59 explicitly refuses to make for the absence direction. The harm is small (a starter profile, self-correcting once the write commits), so I am not filing it as a finding — but the REASONING should not stand, because it is the pattern the round is supposed to be eliminating.
solutions.industrialSolution: Same one-line fix as seam-4: the listener at :46 already passes `includeMetadataChanges: true`, so gate the profile assignment on provenance — accept `snapshot.data(as:)` optimistically for rendering, but only treat the identity as ESTABLISHED (and only clear/settle `statusText`) when `!snapshot.metadata.hasPendingWrites`. Firebase documents that a metadata-opted listener receives a follow-up snapshot with `hasPendingWrites == false` once the write commits, which is the precise event the seed needs. Then the collapsed retry becomes harmless: the seed's `.queuedLocally` return is correct, the listener settles it on commit, and if the write is ultimately rejected the mutation rolls back, a fresh `!exists && !isFromCache` event arrives, and `seedTask == nil` re-arms the seed exactly as the lens describes — but with the intervening state labelled honestly instead of silently.

solutions.findingRef: AUDIT of sound areas — 'REFRESH GENERATION DISCIPLINE — SOUND' (state + flows lenses) is correct but incomplete
solutions.verdictOnFinding: CORRECT AS FAR AS IT GOES. Both lenses assert that every await in `refresh()` is followed by a generation guard (:350, :357, :364, :367, :375, :386, :388) and that there is NO await between the last guard and the publish/retire/reap/reconcile block (:395-431). I verified both claims line by line and they hold; round 6's hoisting of the diagnostics read above the guard in the local-failure branch (:356-359) does genuinely close the previously unguarded failure path. What neither lens follows through: the generation counter protects the PUBLISH against a superseded snapshot, but it does not protect the DESTRUCTIVE decision against a stale premise. `cloudIDs` is computed at :377 from a read that completed before the guard; the retirement at :402-412 consumes it after. `refresh` is invoked from three uncoordinated places (MapScreen.swift:106 on a location-nil flip, DropsListScreen.swift:26, RootView.swift:157) with no mutual exclusion, so the winner of two overlapping refreshes can retire tombstones from a `cloudIDs` snapshot that is already stale by the time it is applied. Low practical risk on its own — but it is a fourth independent reason the retirement predicate must be a per-document positive check rather than a set difference computed across an await boundary, which is why I weight the state-1/flows-1 fix toward `confirmDeleted(id)` over a provenance flag.
solutions.industrialSolution: Do not try to make a set-difference-across-an-await safe with more guards; remove the pattern. Retirement becomes a per-document, server-sourced, same-uid, freshly-evaluated check (`getDocument(source: .server)` → `!exists`) executed at the decision point, bounded by tombstone count. That is correct under any interleaving, needs no additional guard, and does not care how stale the merge-path read was — which is the whole point of preferring a positive check to an inference. Separately, serialise `refresh` with a simple in-flight flag or an actor-isolated task handle so three UI surfaces do not race each other on every tab switch; the generation counter was designed to make a losing refresh harmless, not to make three concurrent refreshes cheap.

research.criticalClosureAudit:
MY OWN CODE-LEVEL AUDIT, derived by reading the files rather than checking the lenses' work.

=== ROUND-5 CRITICAL 1 (reaction loop stranding) — MECHANICALLY CLOSED, DOUBLY. CHARTER OBLIGATION NOT MET. ===

The round-5 defect was that the loop's payoff (wrap → Memory) was gated on a server ack that never arrives offline, because the write awaited a bare continuation Firestore never resumes. Round 6 built TWO independent barriers and both hold:

(a) The write seam is bounded. FirestoreAcked.swift:80-92 races the ack child (:81-84) against an UNCONDITIONAL `Task.sleep` child (:85-88); `group.next()` at :89 resolves on the first completion, so `race` cannot fail to return within `defaultAckTimeout` = 10 s (:29). I grepped the whole target: the only surviving `withCheckedContinuation` in the app is DropEntityFactory.swift:86 (a RealityKit asset load, no Firestore involvement). No continuation remains on any write path. Routing is complete — FirebaseDropStore.swift:75 and :96, ReactionService.swift:53, AccountService.swift:90 and :131 — with exactly one raw write left outside the seam, FirebaseHealthcheck.swift:35, which contradicts the seam's own stated invariant at FirestoreAcked.swift:20 but is diagnostics-only.

(b) The ritual no longer consults the network at all. `didReact` (ReactionSession.swift:55-63) sets `sentEmoji`, `delivery = .sending`, bumps `sendToken`, and calls `startWrap(seconds: 15)` at :60 — zero network reads. `startWrap` (:89-103) is a pure local timer whose only exit assigns `phase = .memory` (:101), and its cancellation handling is correct (`try? await Task.sleep` swallows the CancellationError, the `while remaining > 0, !Task.isCancelled` condition then exits, and the trailing `guard !Task.isCancelled` at :100 prevents a cancelled task promoting to `.memory`). ReactionOverlay's tap handler (:181-197) issues the send in a detached Task AFTER `didReact` has returned the token, so the send cannot delay the wrap. I also confirmed there is no stranded-`.wrapping` path: `wrapTask?.cancel()` is called only from `startWrap` (:90, immediately replaced) and `endSession` (:106, which sets `.idle`).

Even if (a) regressed tomorrow, (b) alone would keep the loop alive. Critical 1's mechanism is closed with redundancy.

BUT the fix RELOCATED the lie rather than removing it, and I rate that a failure of the charter clause the fix was serving. Because the ack deadline (10 s, FirestoreAcked.swift:29) is strictly shorter than the wrap (15 s, ReactionSession.swift:60), `delivery` is ALWAYS settled before `phase == .memory` — deterministically, not racily. RootView.swift:80-89 then constructs MemoryScreen with `myReaction: reactionSession.sentEmoji` and passes no delivery value, and MemoryScreen.swift:137-142 fabricates `DropReaction(emoji: myReaction, uid: "", byName: "")` whenever the cloud fetch (:72) returns empty, rendering "❤️ ×1 from <them>" under "That made <their> day." (:40) with a Save-to-Photos CTA (:58). Round 6 therefore routes 100% of reactions — including hard-rejected ones — to a screen that asserts receipt.

And the frequency is worse than any lens states. `ReactionService.send` throws SYNCHRONOUSLY at :46-49 (`guard AppConfig.firebaseConfigured, let uid = Auth.auth().currentUser?.uid`), before any network. RootView presents ReceiveScreen straight off `.onOpenURL` (:50-73) with no auth gate. So a first-time viewer opening a magic link on a cold launch — the single most common path through this product — can tap on perfect signal, get `.failed` in microseconds, and be handed a confetti keepsake 15 seconds later.

VERDICT: critical 1 CLOSED as a defect; NOT closed as an obligation. The stranding is gone; the lie moved from the lifecycle to the terminal surface, where it is now saveable to the user's photo library.

=== ROUND-5 CRITICAL 2 (immortal tombstone) — LITERAL DEFECT CLOSED AND TESTED; GOVERNING RULE NOT CLOSED. ===

Three retirement mechanisms exist and execute: cloud-read absence (DropStore.swift:402-412, clearing `pendingDeleteIDs` at :404, `unresolvedDeleteIDs` at :409, `deleteAttempts` at :405, with durable clears at :692-695/:702-705); explicit re-receive (:490-494); and the bounded-refusal migration pending→unresolved (:655-659) with `reconcileCloud` replaying only `pendingDeleteIDs` (:568-571). I re-derived that DropStoreTests.swift:479-508 drives exactly three refusals through the `< 3` gate at :569, reaches :655-659, then asserts suppression (:500) and retirement (:507). "Durable and unretirable" is genuinely gone.

It is NOT closed as a class, on four grounds — three of which are wrong PREMISES for the retirement predicate, and one of which is a brand-new violation:

(A) Cache provenance. `cloudReadSucceeded = true` at :376 on any non-throwing return; FirebaseDropStore.swift:32-34 uses the default source and never inspects `snapshot.metadata.isFromCache`. Firestore documents that an offline read is served from cache rather than throwing, and latency compensation has already applied the pending delete to that cache. Every offline delete retires its own tombstone using its own unacknowledged write as the evidence. (state-1/flows-1/seam-2 — correct.)

(B) Owner scoping. `cloudIDs` (:377) derives from `.whereField("ownerUid", isEqualTo: uid)` (FirebaseDropStore.swift:33). Absence means "not mine". Firebase documents that anonymous users receive a new uid on a new device, and the container/UserDefaults are restored from backup while the keychain uid is not. (state-2/flows-2 — correct.)

(C) LOSSY DECODE — MY OWN, found by no lens. `loadDrops` returns `snapshot.documents.compactMap { (try? $0.data(as: CloudDrop.self))?.drop }` (FirebaseDropStore.swift:35-37). `CloudDrop` (:16-21) declares four NON-OPTIONAL stored properties — `drop`, `ownerUid`, `geohash`, `visibility` — and relies on the SYNTHESIZED decoder, so a document missing any one of those keys, or written by a future client or a Cloud Function with a type change, decodes to nil and is silently dropped from `cloudIDs`. A document that demonstrably EXISTS on the server, fetched by a fully server-confirmed read under the correct uid, is therefore treated as absent and retires its tombstone at :403. The same lossiness also hides the row from the merge at :378-383 while `lastSyncError` stays nil (:384), so a schema-drift outage renders as a healthy, empty library. This is precisely the failure class GeoDrop's custom lenient decoder (GeoDrop.swift:103-127, added as "AUDIT P0") was written to prevent — and CloudDrop reintroduces it one layer up, on the path that now makes destructive decisions. Fixing (A) and (B) alone leaves this open.

(D) A NEW SILENT DURABLE STATE. `unresolvedDeleteIDs` (declared :284, persisted :697-705) suppresses user content at :396, is never retried (:568 iterates only `pendingDeleteIDs`), and — I re-ran the grep — appears in DropStore.swift and NO view file. It is retirable, so it does not literally repeat critical 2; but critical 2's rule was "nothing durable may be unretirable," and round 6 closed that while opening "nothing durable may be silent." That is a lateral move, not a fix.

I also note the retirement is over-eager in DIRECTION, which matters for the charter: round 5's bug hid a drop from its owner (annoying, locally recoverable); round 6's bug silently discards the user's delete intent while the content stays link-readable on the server under `allow get: ... (signedIn() && linkVisible())` (rules:40). The new failure is quieter and less recoverable than the one it replaced.

VERDICT: critical 2's literal defect CLOSED and non-vacuously tested; its governing rule NOT closed. Round 6 traded an over-retentive tombstone for an over-eager one built on a predicate that is wrong three independent ways.
crossCutting: CACHE-AS-TRUTH, in three places, with the correct rule already written down once. `cloudReadSucceeded` (DropStore.swift:376) treats a cache-served read as server evidence; `FirestoreAcked.race` returns `.acked` when the stream finishes without yielding (:83), which under cancellation means the local queue, not the server; and the seam lens' own 'seedProfile self-heals' argument accepts a locally-echoed `snapshot.exists` as proof a profile was created (AccountService.swift:49-51). The codebase states the correct rule exactly once, at AccountService.swift:58-61 — 'only a SERVER-confirmed absence means first run', gated on `!snapshot.metadata.isFromCache`. One rule, applied at one seam, everywhere: no destructive action and no confirming UI copy may key on a read or a write outcome the SDK could have satisfied locally.

ABSENCE INFERRED FROM A NARROWED SET. `cloudIDs` is the intersection of three silent narrowings — owner-scoped (FirebaseDropStore.swift:33), successfully-decoded (:35-37, synthesized non-optional CloudDrop), and possibly cache-served (:32-34) — and DropStore.swift:403/:408 read `!cloudIDs.contains(id)` as 'gone from the server'. A negative fact needs a positive check on the specific object (`getDocument(source: .server).exists`), never a set difference over a query. This single substitution closes state-1, state-2, flows-1, flows-2 and the decode hole no lens found.

VERDICTS PRODUCED BY CLIENT PRE-CHECKS INSTEAD OF SERVER STATUS CODES. `ownedByAnotherAccount` (FirebaseDropStore.swift:55-57) is the ONLY producer of terminality, its input (`drop.ownerUid`) is never persisted locally, and every genuine server refusal falls into the generic catch at DropStore.swift:625-628 that keeps the drop pending and re-pushes it on every refresh forever. The whole terminal apparatus — two durable sets, three surfaces, four round-6 tests — is decoration until a gRPC status-code taxonomy exists in FirebaseDropStore. This is the single largest gap between what the app claims to detect and what it can detect, and it will widen the day rules v3 or App Check enforcement lands.

REASSURANCE AS THE FALLTHROUGH BRANCH. ProfileScreen's terminal `else` is 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops' (:104-108); MemoryScreen's empty-fetch fallback fabricates a delivered reaction (:138-140); ShareDropSheet's `else` is 'Sharing makes this drop visible to anyone with the link' (:151-155); FirestoreAcked's stream-exhaustion fallthrough is `.acked` (:83). In a charter whose job is making failure visible, every default, empty and fallthrough branch must resolve to the UNKNOWN state, and the good state must be reachable only by positive evidence. Four instances in one round is a review-checklist item, not four bugs.

TWO HAND-MAINTAINED DEFINITIONS OF ONE CONTRACT. The emoji list (ReactionSession.swift:21 vs firestore.rules:58 — byte-verified drift), the sync-status ladder (ProfileScreen.swift:74-111 vs DropsListScreen.swift:39-69, which round 6 changed on one side only), and the terminal/pending caption precedence recomputed in three views. The team already solved this pattern once and correctly — `watchedDrops`/`listenKey` (ReactionService.swift:75, :91) are a single shared definition specifically so the listener and the SwiftUI task key cannot drift (counsel PBS-3). Every remaining duplicate is a scheduled outage; hoist each to one computed value or generate one side from the other.

NEW DURABLE STATE SHIPPED WITHOUT A SURFACE, A CONTROL, OR A RETIREMENT TEST. `unresolvedDeleteIDs` has none of the three. `terminalSyncFailureIDs` has surfaces but an unreachable producer. `syncFailureReasons` has a round-4 test asserting it is 'visible' and no renderer outside the terminal branch (ShareDropSheet.swift:139) — the state lens correctly flags that test as over-claiming. Proposed gate for round 7: a durable set is not shippable until it has (a) a producer test, (b) a retirement test, (c) a user-visible surface, (d) a user control, and (e) an entry in the 'Synced' precondition.

THE ROUND'S HEADLINE ARTIFACT HAS ZERO EXECUTING TESTS. Every round-6 test reaches the ack states by having `GatedCloudStore` throw `DropStoreError.ackTimedOut` directly (DropStoreTests.swift:436-453), so FirestoreAcked's deadline, its encode-throw→`.rejected` mapping, its cancellation mapping and `race` itself are covered only by reading — and the cancellation mapping is precisely where seam-1 finds the defect. `race` is `private`, so there is no seam to test through. Make the ack source injectable and drive all four outcome mappings; pair it with `@firebase/rules-unit-testing` in CI for the rules half, since the emoji drift is the same untested-contract failure on the server side.

THE SAVE PIPELINE IS HARDENED AND THE DELETE PIPELINE IS NOT. `syncGenerations` guards appear at DropStore.swift:602, :604, :608, :621, :626; there is no `deleteGenerations` anywhere in the file. `launchCloudDelete` (:631-663) has no entry guard, no defer, and a plain trailing `deleteTasks[id] = nil` at :661, and `remove()` (:533) can overwrite an occupied registry slot without cancelling. No field-reachable harm today, but the delete half is the half that now owns the destructive durable decisions (tombstones, the three-strike budget, retirement) — the asymmetry is where the next regression will land.

LATENT PLATFORM RESIDUALS worth recording but not fixing now: (1) `WriteOutcome: Sendable` with an `any Error` payload (FirestoreAcked.swift:12-16) compiles only under Swift 5 language mode and blocks the Swift 6 migration. (2) The durable outbox and tombstone sets live in UserDefaults, whose backing store inherits `NSFileProtectionCompleteUntilFirstUserAuthentication` and reads as EMPTY before the first unlock after boot — and DropLibrary rewrites the whole set on every mark/clear (:707-709), so a pre-first-unlock launch would read empty and then persist empty, destroying the outbox. Unreachable today because Config/Info.plist declares no `UIBackgroundModes` and the app has no push or significant-location entitlement; it becomes data-destroying the day one is added. Apple DTS (Quinn) is explicit: do not rely on UserDefaults in code paths that can execute in the background.
research.shipVerdict:
NOT PRODUCTION-GRADE FOR ITS CHARTER. Wave C's charter is "make failure visible." Round 6 materially improved the plumbing — the write seam is now bounded, cancellable and three-valued; the ritual no longer depends on I/O; the reap keys on a machine-checkable outcome; the vacuous round-4 tests are genuinely fixed. But the charter is judged at the two surfaces where a user asks "did it work?", and both answer "yes" in the failure cases: the Profile status line falls through to "Synced — the server has confirmed your drops" (ProfileScreen.swift:104-108) on every cold launch before the first refresh and after any local-read failure, and the Memory screen asserts receipt for reactions the server rejected (MemoryScreen.swift:137-142). Worse, the one apparatus built to say "no" — `terminalSyncFailureIDs` — has a producer that cannot fire in the field (state-3). The round shipped honest machinery underneath dishonest surfaces, plus a new class of silent durable state.

BLOCKING (six; must land before this ships as a truth surface):
- B1 · state-3 — terminal verdicts have one client-side producer whose input (`drop.ownerUid`) is never persisted, so real server refusals are classified retryable, re-pushed forever, rendered as "Still uploading", and the share sheet hands out a dead link. Blocking because it defeats the wave's central mechanism, is the FIRST thing that fires in the device-migration scenario every other finding assumes, and rules v3 will start producing exactly these refusals on deploy.
- B2 · ux-1 — the Memory screen claims delivery for rejected and queued reactions. Blocking because it is the product's payoff surface, a direct round-6 regression, reachable on a cold link-open with perfect signal via the synchronous `notSignedIn` throw (ReactionService.swift:46-49), and it produces a saved artifact.
- B3 · state-1 / flows-1 / seam-2 — retirement on a cache-served read destroys the delete intent for every offline delete. Blocking because it is silent, unrecoverable, and leaves user-deleted content link-readable on the server.
- B4 · state-4 / ux-4 / flows-6 — "Synced" as a fallthrough. Blocking because it renders on every cold launch and is the literal inverse of the charter. (Note: state-4's stated trigger — a background launch under NSFileProtectionComplete — is unreachable in this app, which declares no background modes; the reachable triggers are more frequent, not less.)
- B5 · seam-3 / ux-2 / flows-3 PLUS the two rules hazards I add — blocks the WAVE A DEPLOY, not the app build. The committed rules file must not be deployed as written: 😂 is denied (byte-verified); `get` on a missing drop now denies instead of returning `exists == false`, breaking `DropSharingService.fetchSharedDrop`'s `snapshot.exists` check; and the reactions `get(drops/…).data.visibility` precondition denies 100% of reactions to any drop shared while offline, at one billed read per attempt.
- B6 · seam-5 / state-5 / ux-5 — `retrySync(sharedDrop)` publishes a share the user was just told failed and desynchronises local from cloud, silently disabling the sender's reaction listener for that drop. One-token fix; blocking because the cost is a keystroke and the harm is a contradiction between statement and behaviour.

NON-BLOCKING (ship with them, scheduled):
- state-2 / flows-2 (uid-stamped tombstones) — severe but device-migration-only, and B3 removes the common trigger. Schedule IMMEDIATELY after B3; it gates the recorded SIWA-linking residual and is the one finding that makes a roadmap target strictly harder.
- ux-3 (unresolvedDeleteIDs has no surface) — non-blocking ONLY IF B3 and state-2 both land, since a sound predicate keeps the set near-empty. If B3 ships alone, PROMOTE TO BLOCKING: a set that is durable, silent, content-suppressing and never retried is exactly what the charter forbids.
- seam-1 (cancellation → `.acked`) — I verified zero reachable harm today: the only two cancellation sites bump `syncGenerations` first and `performCloudSync` re-checks; the three unguarded consumers never cancel. Two-line fix; land it alongside the B-work so it cannot become reachable.
- seam-4 (no late-ack re-check) — degrades honesty for minutes, always in the under-claiming direction, except AccountService's permanently stuck `statusText`. Take the one-line `hasPendingWrites` fix in the profile listener now; defer the rest into the listener-diff residual.
- state-6 (receivedViaLink as ownership) — needs the persisted ownerUid that B1 introduces, so it is a natural follow-on. Take the interim one-liner (clear the flag when the fetched ownerUid equals the current uid) inside B1's PR.
- ux-6 (Dismiss race) — real in both orderings and it leaves disk and screen disagreeing, but self-heals on the next refresh in one of the two. Small, low-risk fix.
- flows-4 (late reactions never toast) — non-blocking on its own; it is the sender-side half of B2, so after B2 the viewer at least knows the truth. Schedule with the `serverTimestamp` + `documentChanges` change.
- flows-5 (revalidation is a no-op) — non-blocking once B6 changes what is passed, but the COPY must change with B1 or the app keeps offering a retry it cannot perform.
- seam-6 (dead `notFound` branch) — comment and dead code; fold into B3's delete work, along with the "never tombstone a never-acked drop" guard that removes three wasted refusals per case.
- Recorded residuals, not findings: `WriteOutcome: Sendable` with an `any Error` payload blocks the Swift 6 migration; FirebaseHealthcheck.swift:35 is a raw write contradicting the seam's own invariant; `CloudDrop`'s synthesized strict decoder reintroduces the failure class GeoDrop's custom decoder fixed, on the path that now makes destructive decisions; UserDefaults-backed durable sets are unreadable before first unlock (Apple DTS) — harmless today, data-destroying the day a background mode is added; the delete pipeline has none of the save pipeline's generation discipline.

THE SINGLE NEXT ACTION: fix the terminal-verdict producer (B1). In `FirebaseDropStore.save`, map `NSError(FirestoreErrorDomain, …)` non-retryable gRPC codes — PERMISSION_DENIED, UNAUTHENTICATED, INVALID_ARGUMENT, FAILED_PRECONDITION, NOT_FOUND — to a new `DropStoreError.refusedByServer(reason)`; add the matching catch beside DropStore.swift:618; and persist the stamped `ownerUid` back through `local.save` after a successful upload. Nothing else in the backlog changes as much per line. It converts `terminalSyncFailureIDs`, the xmark badge, the Profile branch, the ShareDropSheet refusal and four of the round's eight tests from decoration into a working verdict path; it stops an unbounded re-push loop that App Check enforcement would turn into a library-wide storm; it supplies the durable input that state-6 and flows-5 both need; and it is a precondition for the Wave A rules deploy, which will generate precisely these refusals. Carry B2 and B6 in the same PR — both are small, both are lies on shipping surfaces, and B2's display fix only becomes meaningful once the verdicts beneath it are true.
